articles.body_html:
Jev labels the line. Code makes the call.

TL;DR: README Clew 2 checks whether a public GitHub README matches its code, for JavaScript and TypeScript repos. A small decision model called Jev labels what kind of claim each README line is, five fixed code checks decide whether it's true, and Claude Haiku writes the summary. I built it in five days with AdaL, SylphAI's coding agent, for AdaL's "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon. Its first real test was my own old repo, and it got it wrong.

AdaL's "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon asked for one thing: build a project with AdaL, the coding agent from SylphAI, that puts Jev to real use. I didn't have a problem to solve. I had a model, and a deadline.

Jev is a small decision model from TypeSafe. DigitalOcean's write-up calls it "an AI model that can't write a sentence," and that's the point of it. You give it a question, the rules for answering, and a fixed set of labels. It picks one label and tells you how sure it is, as a number between 0 and 1. You reach it through Glasser, which runs Jev calls and charges per call.

That's an odd tool to start from. My builds usually start with a problem, and then I pick a model. This one started with the model, so I went looking for a problem that fit it. My first thought was to rework apps from my Hot AR Summer run, since they're already deterministic. Then I went through a lot more. Dewey. Pun Court. Sortes. Which Door. Saint of Small Things, which I love too much to shoehorn into a format it doesn't fit. I ruled out legal tools too. Every fun idea died on the same line in the judging criteria: "a clear reason the project should exist."

So I went back to a reason I already had. In May I built README Clew because I always worried my READMEs disagreed with my own repos. It worked, and its own README listed two honest limits. Claude was asked to quote the README word for word, which was a prompt rule, not a code check. And it sometimes read prose labels like "Frontend (Vite)" as package names, which produced false accusations.

Both limits are labeling problems. Labeling is the one thing Jev does.

A clew, said like "clue," is a ball of thread. In the Greek myth, Ariadne gave Theseus one so he could follow it back out of the Labyrinth. README Clew follows the thread from each README line back to the code. It's also the name of my Clew Suite of civic tech tools.

earlgreyhot1701D / readme-clew-2

Checks whether your README matches your code. Chrome extension + web page for any public JS/TS repo. Rules and five deterministic verifiers decide what's true, Jev labels README lines with calibrated confidence, Haiku explains the findings. Line-linked receipts, status badge, JSON export. Built with AdaL for What Would Jev Do?

README Clew 2

Checks whether a GitHub README matches its code.

Live: https://readme-clew-2.vercel.app

Paste a public JavaScript or TypeScript repo, press SCAN, and get a claim ledger: every checkable line of the README, what the code says about it, and who decided.

Built for the AdaL "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon, October 6 to 11, 2026.

Why "clew"? A clew (said like "clue") is a ball of thread. In the Greek myth, Ariadne gave Theseus a clew so he could follow it back out of the Labyrinth, and it's where the word "clue" comes from. README Clew follows the thread from each README line back to the code. It's also the name of the author's suite of civic tech tools.

What it does

READMEs drift. A command gets renamed, an env var gets dropped, a package gets swapped, and the README keeps promising the old thing. README Clew 2 reads…

View on GitHub

What it does

READMEs drift. A command gets renamed, an env var gets dropped, a package gets swapped, and the README keeps promising the old thing. README Clew 2 reads the README line by line and sorts every line into one of four buckets:

Bucket Means
Contradicted The README says it, the code disagrees
Missing The code does it, the README never mentions it
Unverifiable No code check can test it, or Jev wasn't sure what kind of line it was
Verified The README and the code agree

Every row shows the exact README line, the code evidence, and who decided: a rule or Jev.

That's a real scan of v1. No contradictions, and four packages the code imports that the README never names. The new version audits the old one.

Jev never gets the last word

The rule I built around: models never decide what's true.

Code splits the README into lines and settles the easy ones without any model: headings, badges, blank lines. For the rest, Jev picks what kind of claim the line is. A dependency, a command, an env var, a file or URL, or something no code check covers.

A line only goes to a code check if Jev is at least 0.8 confident it's one of the four checkable kinds. Below that, it lands in Unverifiable, tagged "Jev wasn't sure." Then five deterministic verifiers read package.json, the file tree and the source, and decide. Same input, same answer. Claude Haiku writes a short summary at the end from counts and names only. It never sees the README lines, so a README with planted instructions can't talk to it.

The two mistakes aren't equal. Calling a line Unverifiable costs a little coverage. Calling a correct line Contradicted costs your trust. I took that framing from Swift at MLH, who published I got Jev to zero mistakes. I'm still using Flash-Lite. the same day I was writing Jev's questions. His lessons reshaped the build: describe what each checker can't see instead of what a README line looks like, give Jev no worked examples, and count mistakes per line instead of per run.

My twist was to turn the scariest failure into code instead of a prompt. A package name that only shows up in prose can never be marked Contradicted, no matter how sure Jev is.

On a held-out set of 32 README lines, run twice with the settings frozen:

Measure Run 1 Run 2
Wrong labels that got past the 0.8 bar 0 0
False Contradicted, end to end 0 0
Real drift found 3 of 3 3 of 3

Thirty-two lines is a small sample. It supports "safe enough to ship," not a measured error rate.

A full scan costs about a penny. Roughly $0.009 of that is Jev.

One agent, one build log

I direct, validate and decide. AdaL wrote the code and the tests, ran the Jev evaluation, deployed to Vercel, and drove a real browser for QA. Claude (Opus 5.5) wrote the spec and the architecture, reviewed AdaL's work at every checkpoint, and wrote the docs.

AdaL worked from an AGENTS.md it read every turn: propose first, one block at a time, touch only the files named, stop for a QA checkpoint. My last build left me with a 1,200-line god file, so this one had a 200-line cap per file, enforced by a test that fails the suite. A rule in a prompt is only a request. A failing test is a rule.

AdaL followed all of it, and it was fast. In plan mode it proposed and confirmed plans so quickly that I'd paste a prompt, step away, and come back to finished work. It also found real bugs nobody told it to look for:

  • Glasser, the service that runs Jev calls, caps a call at 100 questions. Only the live API says so, not the schema.
  • A timer that let tests quietly cancel instead of fail.
  • A trimmer measuring the wrong version of the text.
  • Two layout bugs that only showed up in a real browser. That last one surprised me. AdaL switched on its own browser tool to screenshot and time the page. I never toggled it.

Not everything was smooth. AdaL sat on "Create lib/report.js" for 22 minutes after the file was written and every test had passed. Only the screen was stuck. My laptop fan has gone off more this week than in the last year. Glasser's connector inside AdaL broke every Claude call until I turned it off and reported it. And on day four, right after I approved the biggest block, my weekly plan credits ran out.

The fix was in AdaL's own docs: bring your own API key. I already had Claude API credits. About 35 minutes later AdaL was building again on my key.

The AdaL team deserves its own paragraph. They fixed the Glasser connector the same day I reported it. When I told them I'd hit the weekly limit, they granted a credit so I could finish. This is the first hackathon where I've had direct, fast contact with the people running it, and it made a five-day sprint feel less lonely.

The mascot shows the split too. AdaL drew the first clew in code, as SVG faces, then two thread-ball styles to pick from. The one that shipped was painted by ChatGPT, then cut out and sized by Claude. An agent that draws with paths and an image model that paints are good at different things.

It's me, I'm the problem

Apart from the connector bug, most of the friction in this build was me.

I'm terrified of shipping slop, so I asked for every test to be shown failing once. Break the code on purpose, watch the test go red, restore it. In Block 1 that meant 102 tests and 75 deliberate breaks. Then it kept going.

Point in the build Tests
Block 1 102
Blocks 3 and 4 197
Monorepo fix 222
Before the UI polish 353
Saturday night 452
Submission 474

Some of those tests matter a lot. The ones that guard the five checkers, the 0.8 bar, the prose rule and the monorepo regressions are the ones keeping a correct README from being called wrong. A lot of the rest re-prove page wiring that the browser checks already covered. For a five-day build, that's ridiculous.

It also cost real money. Every deliberate break is a full test run, and every run is agent time. My second rookie mistake was never starting a new AdaL session. Every turn resends the whole conversation, so the later turns of a long session cost the most. By Saturday night I'd spent $36 of the $50 cap I set on my key in about three and a half hours.

AdaL did exactly what the prompts asked. The guidance set the bar, mine and Claude's.

The fix was a "lean mode" header at the top of each prompt: a fresh session per block, read only the files you need, show failing once per new test file instead of per test, run browser QA once at the end. The rest of the build, hardening, the extension, the README and the last fixes, cost about $4. The final bill for the agent was $40.35. The app costs about a penny a scan.

Next time I'll set a test budget per block before the block starts, and match it to what a failure would cost a user, not to habit.

The first thing it got wrong was mine

The first real scan was my own v1 repo. README Clew 2 called three lines Contradicted and flagged four packages as Missing. Claude opened v1's files to check. All seven were false.

v1 is a pnpm monorepo, with workspaces in folders the workspace finder didn't know about. And pnpm's --filter option was being read as a script name. The tool was wrong in exactly the way it promises never to be, on my own repo, a few hours before any judge saw it.

AdaL fixed it in one block. Anything it can't resolve now comes back Unverifiable, never Contradicted, and v1 became a saved regression test. On the rescan: Contradicted went from 3 to 0, and the four Missing packages turned out to be real.

A second live scan, of the polka repo, found 14 Missing packages that all came from an examples folder with its own package file. Same fix, same kind of test.

The last two came from a question I asked late Saturday: did we build for false contradictions? Claude reread every checker and found two more ways to accuse a correct README. An env var used in a file past the 20-file read limit. And a README pointing at build output like dist/, which is never committed. AdaL made both come back Unverifiable.

The last bugs came from asking the question the tool exists to answer.

What it can't do

  • JavaScript and TypeScript only. In JS and TS, one file, package.json, lists both the packages and the commands. Python spreads the same facts across several optional files. A repo with no package.json gets a clear message, and no model is called.
  • Most lines end up Unverifiable. Most README text is prose no code check can test. Unverifiable means "can't tell," not "wrong."
  • Monorepo support covers simple workspace patterns and up to 30 workspaces. Beyond that, Missing turns into Unverifiable.
  • It reads at most 20 source files per scan, and cuts READMEs over 50 KB.
  • The same README scanned twice can move one borderline line between buckets. The 0.8 bar keeps that drift away from Contradicted.
  • No README badge. A badge would re-run a scan and bill me every time someone viewed it, and with no storage there's no safe way to cache it. ## Try it

There are three ways in, and they all hit the same scan:

Way Best when
Live page You want the full ledger, or you're on a phone. No install
Chrome extension You're already on the repo's GitHub page. One click
Bookmarklet You can't install extensions, like on a locked-down work computer. Drag it from the ABOUT tab

The bookmarklet is there because of my day job. Work computers block extensions, and a bookmark that opens the page with the repo filled in gets past that.

There's no database and no account. Scans are never stored, and logs keep counts and timing only. Since nothing is kept, DOWNLOAD JSON gives you the report as a file, with a scan receipt: the repo and commit, a fingerprint of the README text, and a fingerprint of the report so you can tell later if it was edited. No model writes any of it. Attach it to a pull request, or keep it as a before-and-after.

Before I submitted, README Clew 2 scanned its own README: 285 lines, 154 sent to Jev, 5.6 seconds. 0 Contradicted, 0 Missing, 1 Verified, and 107 Unverifiable. The one Verified line is npm test, and package.json does have a test script. The 107 is the honest number. Most of a README is prose. On "Built for the AdaL 'What Would Jev Do?' hackathon," Jev said not a checkable claim, 0.52 sure, and the line never went near a checker.

Press USE DEMO REPO, then SCAN, and watch the new version grade the old one. The code, the decision log and every wrong turn are in the repo.

Quick context if you are new here. I work in the California courts, running court operations for the county. I started building with AI in July 2025 and I have been learning in public ever since. I do not write the code. I direct, the agents generate, I validate and decide.

Built with AI assistance in October 2026 for the AdaL "What Would Jev Do?" hackathon, with Jev by TypeSafe called through Glasser. These tools move fast, so check the source before you quote me.

AI Assisted. Human Approved. Powered by NLP.

articles.title: TypeScript `TemplateStringsArray` and Tagged Templates: Building Type-Safe DSLs in 2026
articles.description: Master tagged template literals and TemplateStringsArray to build type-safe domain-specific languages in TypeScript. Learn production patterns for HTML sanitization, SQL builders, and internationalization.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript TemplateStringsArray and Tagged Templates: Building Type-Safe DSLs in 2026

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

Most template literal problems stem from treating dynamic strings as if they were simple concatenation. Teams reach for template literals when they need interpolation, but miss the deeper capability: tagged templates transform template literals into structured, type-safe function calls. The distinction matters because ordinary template literals lose all type information about their interpolated values, while tagged templates preserve and enforce those types at compile time.

The pattern that production codebases overlook is the TemplateStringsArray type. This built-in TypeScript type exposes the raw structure of template literals, giving developers the foundation to build domain-specific languages that catch errors before runtime. When a function tags a template literal, TypeScript passes the static string fragments as a TemplateStringsArray and the interpolated values as separate typed parameters.

The alternative approach wraps template literals with tag functions that enforce constraints at the type level. A tagged template receives the literal parts and interpolated expressions as distinct arguments, allowing the tag function to validate, transform, or reject values before constructing the final output.

Key Takeaways

  • TemplateStringsArray exposes the static string fragments of a template literal as a read-only array with a raw property containing unescaped versions.
  • Tagged template functions receive string fragments and interpolated values as separate parameters, enabling type-safe validation and transformation before output construction.
  • Production DSLs for HTML sanitization, SQL queries, and internationalization rely on tagged templates to prevent injection attacks and enforce structural constraints at compile time.
  • The choice between tagged templates and function calls depends on whether the syntax benefits from literal-first structure or whether runtime flexibility matters more than ergonomic syntax.
  • Raw string access through TemplateStringsArray.raw preserves escape sequences, critical for tools that generate code or process strings with literal backslashes.

Understanding TemplateStringsArray: The Hidden First Parameter

When a function tags a template literal, TypeScript invokes it with a specialized first argument of type TemplateStringsArray. This type represents the static string fragments between interpolation points, always containing one more element than the number of interpolated values.

The structure carries two critical properties. The array itself holds processed string fragments where escape sequences like \n become actual newlines. The raw property contains an identical array but with escape sequences preserved as literal characters. This distinction matters when building tools that generate source code or process strings where backslashes carry meaning.

function inspect(strings: TemplateStringsArray, ...values: unknown[]): void {
  console.log('Processed:', strings);
  console.log('Raw:', strings.raw);
  console.log('Values:', values);
}

const name = 'Alice';
const age = 30;

inspect`User: ${name}\nAge: ${age}`;
// Processed: [ 'User: ', '\nAge: ', '' ]
// Raw: [ 'User: ', '\\nAge: ', '' ]
// Values: [ 'Alice', 30 ]

The empty string at the end of the fragments array appears because the template literal ends immediately after the final interpolation. Every interpolation point creates a boundary: the fragment before it, the interpolated value, and the fragment after it. A template literal with no interpolations produces an array with a single element.

The raw property exists specifically for scenarios where the developer needs the original source representation. A code generator that emits JavaScript must preserve backslashes in string literals. A regex builder that constructs patterns from template literals needs literal backslashes for escape sequences. Without access to raw strings, these tools would require users to double-escape every backslash, breaking the ergonomic benefit of template literals.

The type definition of TemplateStringsArray extends ReadonlyArray<string> and adds the raw property as a readonly string array. This inheritance means standard array methods like map, join, and slice work on the fragments, but mutation methods throw type errors. The immutability enforces a constraint: tag functions should not modify the input structure, only process it to produce output.

Building a Type-Safe HTML Sanitizer with Tagged Templates

HTML injection vulnerabilities occur when user input enters markup without escaping special characters. The classic mistake treats all interpolated values identically, allowing `` tags or event handlers to execute in the browser. A tagged template function can enforce escaping at the type level, rejecting values that have not been explicitly marked as safe.

`typescript
type SafeHTML = { __brand: 'SafeHTML'; value: string };

function escapeHTML(str: string): string {
return str
.replace(/&/g, '&')
.replace(/ .replace(/>/g, '>')
.replace(/"/g, '"')
.replace(/'/g, ''');
}

function markSafe(html: string): SafeHTML {
return { __brand: 'SafeHTML', value: html };
}

function html(
strings: TemplateStringsArray,
...values: (string | SafeHTML)[]
): SafeHTML {
let result = strings[0];

for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
const value = values[i];
const safeValue = typeof value === 'string'
? escapeHTML(value)
: value.value;
result += safeValue + strings[i + 1];
}

return markSafe(result);
}

// Usage
const userName = 'alert("XSS")';
const title = markSafe('Welcome');

const page = html
<h1>${title}</h1>
<p>Hello, ${userName}!</p>
;

console.log(page.value);
//

Welcome


//

Hello, <script>alert("XSS")</script>!


`

The SafeHTML branded type prevents accidental bypasses. A developer cannot pass raw HTML markup without explicitly calling markSafe, which signals intentional opt-in to unescaped content. The tag function checks each interpolated value: plain strings get escaped automatically, while SafeHTML values pass through unchanged.

This pattern extends to component libraries and templating systems. A framework might provide tag functions for different contexts: html for markup, css for styles, sql for queries. Each enforces context-appropriate escaping rules, and TypeScript prevents mixing values across contexts. The type system becomes a security boundary, not just documentation.

The failure mode here is subtle but expensive. Without type-level protection, a developer might forget to escape a single interpolation point, creating a vector for code injection. Manual code review catches some instances, but tagged templates eliminate the entire category of error. The compiler enforces safety, and unsafe operations require explicit opt-in.

Creating a SQL Query Builder DSL with Full Type Safety

SQL injection remains a persistent vulnerability because string concatenation cannot distinguish between query structure and user input. Prepared statements solve this problem by sending parameters separately from the query text, but building them manually with placeholder indices creates maintenance burden. A tagged template can automate placeholder generation while preserving full type safety.

`typescript
interface SQLQuery {
text: string;
values: unknown[];
}

function sql(
strings: TemplateStringsArray,
...values: unknown[]
): SQLQuery {
let text = strings[0];

for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
text += $${i + 1}${strings[i + 1]};
}

return { text, values };
}

// Usage with typed parameters
interface User {
id: number;
email: string;
}

async function findUser(email: string): Promise {
const query = sql
SELECT id, email
FROM users
WHERE email = ${email}
AND deleted_at IS NULL
;

// query.text: 'SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE email = $1 AND deleted_at IS NULL'
// query.values: ['user@example.com']

const result = await db.query(query.text, query.values);
return result.rows[0] ?? null;
}
`

The tag function constructs parameterized queries by replacing each interpolation point with a numbered placeholder. The database driver receives the query text and values as separate arguments, preventing any possibility of injection. The interpolated values never merge into the SQL string itself.

Advanced query builders extend this pattern with type inference. By analyzing the table schema, the builder can enforce that column names exist and that WHERE clause values match column types. A query that references a non-existent column or passes a string where an integer belongs fails at compile time.

`typescript
type ColumnType = T extends number ? number
: T extends string ? string
: T extends boolean ? boolean
: never;

type WhereClause = {
[K in keyof T]?: ColumnType | ColumnType[];
};

function buildWhere(
strings: TemplateStringsArray,
...values: Array>
): SQLQuery {
// Implementation details omitted for brevity
return { text: '', values };
}

interface Product {
id: number;
name: string;
price: number;
active: boolean;
}

// Type-safe: price is number
const validQuery = sqlSELECT * FROM products WHERE price < ${100};

// Type error: string not assignable to number
// const invalidQuery = sqlSELECT * FROM products WHERE price < ${"100"};
`

Production query builders combine tagged templates with schema introspection. Tools like Prisma or Kysely generate TypeScript types from database schemas, then use those types to validate queries at compile time. The tag function becomes a bridge between the runtime query execution and the compile-time type guarantees.

The implication here is that type safety extends beyond the application code into the database layer. A refactoring that renames a column or changes a type triggers compiler errors in every affected query. The feedback loop shortens from runtime crashes or integration test failures to immediate red squiggles in the editor.

Tagged Templates vs Function Calls: When Each Approach Wins

The decision between tagged templates and regular function calls comes down to syntax ergonomics versus runtime flexibility. Tagged templates excel when the static structure of the input matters more than dynamic composition, while function calls win when the construction logic needs conditional branches or loops.

Tagged templates enforce a literal-first API. The template string must appear at the call site, not constructed dynamically from variables. This constraint prevents accidentally building unsafe strings at runtime, but it also limits expressiveness. A query builder that needs to construct WHERE clauses from an unknown number of conditions cannot use tagged templates alone.

Function calls provide full runtime flexibility. A builder function can accept arrays of conditions, loop over them to construct clauses, and conditionally include fragments based on runtime values. The tradeoff is that the function cannot leverage TypeScript's template literal type inference, so type safety requires explicit generic parameters or overloads.

`typescript
// Tagged template: ergonomic but inflexible
const query1 = sql
SELECT * FROM users
WHERE email = ${email}
AND age > ${minAge}
;

// Function call: flexible but verbose
interface QueryBuilder {
table(name: string): QueryBuilder;
where(column: string, value: unknown): QueryBuilder;
build(): SQLQuery;
}

const query2 = new QueryBuilder()
.table('users')
.where('email', email)
.where('age', minAge)
.build();
`

The pattern that works in production combines both approaches. Use tagged templates for the common case where developers write literal queries, and provide escape hatches for dynamic construction. A query builder might expose both a sql tag function and a sql.dynamic() method that accepts an array of fragments and values.

Libraries like styled-components demonstrate this hybrid approach. The primary API uses tagged templates for ergonomic component styling, but the library also exports functions for runtime theme logic and conditional styles. Developers reach for the tagged template 90% of the time, and the function API covers edge cases.

The failure mode is forcing tagged templates into scenarios where they do not fit. A developer who tries to build a dynamic query by concatenating template literals defeats the entire safety mechanism. The correct solution recognizes when the use case needs runtime flexibility and switches to an appropriate API that maintains type safety through different mechanisms.

Production Patterns: Internationalization, Routing, and Styled Components

Internationalization libraries use tagged templates to enforce placeholder consistency across translations. A translation key must interpolate the same variables in every language, preventing runtime errors where a translation references a missing parameter. The tag function validates that every interpolation point has a corresponding value in the provided object.

`typescript
type TranslationKey = {
en: string;
es: string;
fr: string;
};

function t(
strings: TemplateStringsArray,
...keys: string[]
): (values: Record) => string {
return (values) => {
const locale = getCurrentLocale();
const translations: Record = getTranslations();

let result = strings[0];
for (let i = 0; i < keys.length; i++) {
  const key = keys[i];
  if (!(key in values)) {
    throw new Error(`Missing translation value: ${key}`);
  }
  result += String(values[key]) + strings[i + 1];
}

return result;

};
}

// Define translations
const greeting = tHello, ${'name'}! You have ${'count'} messages.;

// Use with values
console.log(greeting({ name: 'Alice', count: 5 }));
// "Hello, Alice! You have 5 messages."
`

Type-safe routing libraries leverage tagged templates to generate URLs with compile-time guarantees that all parameters exist. A route template defines the structure, and the tag function ensures that every dynamic segment receives a value when generating a URL. The type system prevents typos in parameter names and catches missing values.

Styled-components pioneered the use of tagged templates for CSS-in-JS. The library interprets template literals as CSS text, provides editor highlighting and autocomplete, and generates optimized stylesheets at runtime. Interpolated values can reference theme objects, component props, or dynamic calculations, all with full TypeScript support.

`typescript
import styled from 'styled-components';

interface ButtonProps {
variant: 'primary' | 'secondary';
size: 'small' | 'large';
}

const Button = styled.button`
padding: ${props => props.size === 'small' ? '8px 16px' : '12px 24px'};
background-color: ${props =>
props.variant === 'primary' ? '#007bff' : '#6c757d'
};
color: white;
border: none;
border-radius: 4px;
font-size: ${props => props.size === 'small' ? '14px' : '16px'};

&:hover {
opacity: 0.8;
}
`;

// Usage with type-safe props
Click me
`

The critical insight across these patterns is that tagged templates provide a DSL that feels like native syntax while maintaining full TypeScript type checking. A developer writing a translation key, a route path, or a styled component uses familiar template literal syntax, but the compiler enforces domain-specific constraints that plain strings cannot express.

Production codebases benefit most when the tagged template API aligns with the domain model. Internationalization naturally maps to template literals with named placeholders. Route definitions read like URL patterns with dynamic segments. CSS-in-JS mirrors the structure of actual stylesheets. The ergonomics come from matching the syntax to the problem domain.

Common Pitfalls: Type Inference, Raw Strings, and Security

Type inference for tagged templates fails when TypeScript cannot determine the relationship between string fragments and interpolated values. A tag function that returns a complex union type might produce any or overly broad types if the function signature does not guide the compiler. The solution is explicit generic parameters or overloads that narrow the return type based on the input.

`typescript
// Poor: loses type information
function query(strings: TemplateStringsArray, ...values: unknown[]): unknown {
// Implementation
return {};
}

const result = querySELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${1};
// result: unknown

// Better: explicit return type
function queryTyped(
strings: TemplateStringsArray,
...values: unknown[]
): T {
// Implementation
return {} as T;
}

interface User {
id: number;
email: string;
}

const typedResult = queryTypedSELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${1};
// typedResult: User
`

Raw string access through TemplateStringsArray.raw exposes escape sequences, but developers often forget that this property exists. A tag function that builds regular expressions or generates code needs raw strings to preserve backslashes. Using the processed strings produces incorrect output because \n becomes a newline instead of a literal backslash followed by n.

Security vulnerabilities emerge when developers bypass the safety mechanisms of tagged templates. A function that accepts both tagged templates and plain strings cannot distinguish between sanitized and unsanitized input. The type system offers no protection if the implementation treats all strings identically.

`typescript
// Dangerous: accepts both tagged and untagged strings
function dangerousHTML(
input: TemplateStringsArray | string,
...values: unknown[]
): string {
if (typeof input === 'string') {
return input; // No sanitization!
}
// Tagged template path with sanitization
let result = input[0];
for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
result += escapeHTML(String(values[i])) + input[i + 1];
}
return result;
}

// This compiles but bypasses sanitization
const unsafe = dangerousHTML('alert("XSS")');
`

The correct approach splits the API: one function accepts tagged templates and enforces safety, while a separate function handles plain strings but requires explicit acknowledgment of the risk. The type signatures prevent accidental mixing, and naming conventions signal the security implications.

Performance considerations matter when tag functions execute inside hot paths. Each tagged template invocation allocates a new array for the string fragments and another for the interpolated values. A tag function called thousands of times per second can create garbage collection pressure. Memoization or pooling strategies mitigate this cost in performance-critical code.

`typescript
const cache = new Map();

function memoizedTag(
strings: TemplateStringsArray,
...values: unknown[]
): string {
let result = cache.get(strings);

if (!result) {
result = strings[0];
for (let i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {
result += \${${i}} + strings[i + 1];
}
cache.set(strings, result);
}

return result.replace(/\${(\d+)}/g, (_, i) => String(values[i]));
}
`

The failure mode here is assuming that tagged templates come with no runtime cost. The convenience of the syntax hides allocations and function calls that add up in aggregate. Profiling reveals whether the overhead matters for a specific use case, and optimization techniques exist when it does.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between TemplateStringsArray and a regular string array?

TemplateStringsArray is a read-only array type that adds a raw property containing the original string fragments with escape sequences preserved. Regular string arrays are mutable and lack this property. TypeScript uses TemplateStringsArray specifically for the first parameter of tagged template functions to provide access to both processed and raw string data.

Can tagged template functions return promises or other async values?

Tagged template functions can return any type including promises. The tag function signature determines the return type, and callers must handle it appropriately. Async tag functions enable use cases like database queries that need to await results before returning the final value. The await keyword works naturally with promises returned from tagged templates.

How do tagged templates handle nested template literals?

Nested template literals evaluate from the inside out. The innermost template literal executes first, produces a string, and that string becomes an interpolated value in the outer template. If the outer template has a tag function, it receives the fully evaluated inner result as one of its value parameters. Each level of nesting creates a separate function invocation with its own TemplateStringsArray.

Why does TemplateStringsArray extend ReadonlyArray instead of Array?

The immutability constraint prevents tag functions from modifying the input structure. Since the template literal syntax is static at the call site, allowing mutations would create confusion between the source code representation and the runtime value. The compiler enforces that tag functions treat the string fragments as immutable data.

Can you use tagged templates with generic type parameters?

Tagged template functions support generic type parameters like any other function. The generics can constrain the types of interpolated values or determine the return type based on input types. Type inference works best when the generic parameters have clear relationships to the function signature, allowing TypeScript to infer types without explicit annotations at the call site.

Conclusion: When Tagged Templates Are the Right Tool

Tagged templates solve a specific category of problem: building domain-specific languages where syntax ergonomics matter and type safety cannot compromise. The pattern works when the structure of the input is known at write time and the interpolated values need validation or transformation before output construction.

Production use cases fall into three categories: preventing injection attacks through automatic escaping, enforcing structural constraints like parameter presence, and providing familiar syntax for specialized domains. HTML sanitizers, SQL builders, internationalization systems, routing libraries, and CSS-in-JS all benefit from the combination of readable syntax and compile-time guarantees.

The tradeoff is loss of runtime flexibility. Tagged templates cannot express logic that depends on dynamic conditions or loops over collections. When a use case needs that flexibility, function-based APIs remain the better choice. The decision comes down to whether the syntax benefits justify the constraints.

That covers the essential patterns for TypeScript tagged templates and TemplateStringsArray. Apply these in production and the difference will be immediate: fewer runtime errors, better developer experience, and type-safe DSLs that feel like native language features.

articles.title: A single console.log was costing us $40,000 a year. I found it by accident.
articles.description: Our API was slow. Not down, not throwing — just mysteriously, expensively slow under load. The p99...
articles.body_html:
Our API was slow. Not down, not throwing — just mysteriously, expensively slow under load. The p99 crept up month over month. We scaled out servers to keep latency sane. The cloud bill climbed. Everyone had a theory and nobody had a cause.

We blamed the database. We blamed the ORM. We blamed the new framework version. We blamed, briefly and unfairly, the intern.

The actual culprit was a line none of us would have looked at twice:

logger.info(`Request payload: ${JSON.stringify(req.body)}`)

I only found it because I was profiling something else. That's the part that still bothers me.

Why a log line nobody reads can still cost you money

Here's the thing that line does that isn't obvious: it does all its work before the logger gets a vote.

In production our log level was warn. So logger.info(...) was a no-op — the logger took the finished string, checked the level, and dropped it on the floor. Every time. We were paying full price to build a thing we had already decided to throw away.

Walk through what "build it" means on a hot path that runs on every single request:

  1. JSON.stringify(req.body) serializes the entire request body. Some of ours were small. Some were a few hundred KB of nested arrays.
  2. The template literal concatenates that into a new string — another full copy in memory.
  3. All of that garbage gets allocated, then handed to the logger, which looks at the level and says "nope," and now the garbage collector has to clean up megabytes of strings nobody ever saw.

The logging was free. The preparing to log was the tax. And we paid it on every request, forever, for output that physically never left the process.

The rule: your code isn't just what it computes. It's also what it prepares to compute and then discards. On a cold path that's invisible. On a hot path it's the bill.

How it hid for so long

This is the uncomfortable part, because the line is correct. It compiles, it does exactly what it says, it passed review (I approved it). In a unit test it's instant — one call, tiny payload, who'd notice.

It only becomes a problem at the intersection of three things that no single person was looking at together:

  • it's on a path that runs on every request (volume),
  • the payload is sometimes large (cost per call),
  • the log level means the result is always thrown away (pure waste).

Each of those is fine alone. Stacked, they turned a debugging convenience into a line item. And because the symptom was "the whole service is a bit slow and a bit expensive," it pointed at everything except the one line responsible. Slowness with no single owner is the hardest kind to find — there's no stack trace for "death by a thousand allocations."

The rule: the expensive bugs aren't the ones that break something. They're the ones that quietly tax something that runs a million times a day.

The one-line fix

The fix is to stop building the string yourself and let the logger decide whether it's even worth building.

// ❌ Builds and serializes the string ALWAYS — even when it's dropped
logger.info(`Request payload: ${JSON.stringify(req.body)}`)

// ✅ Pass the object. The logger serializes lazily — only if this level will log.
logger.info('Request payload: %o', req.body)

Pass the object, not a pre-built string. Now the serialization is the logger's problem, and a decent logger only does it if the level is actually going to print. At warn in prod, req.body is never touched. At debug locally, you get your full payload. Same code, and the cost appears exactly when the value does.

If your logger doesn't support lazy args, the explicit guard does the same job:

if (logger.isLevelEnabled('info')) {
  logger.info(`Request payload: ${JSON.stringify(req.body)}`)
}

Uglier, but it makes the point visible: nothing gets built unless someone's going to read it.

What changed

I'm not going to hand you a fake precision — I'll tell you the shape of it, because the shape is the lesson.

  • p99 latency dropped sharply once the per-request allocation and GC pressure went away. The service stopped doing a pile of pointless work on the critical path.
  • We scaled back down. We'd been running extra instances purely to absorb the overhead of garbage we generated and deleted. Those instances came off.
  • Annualized, the instance reduction was in the tens of thousands of dollars. For us it rounded to about $40k/year — not from a clever optimization, but from deleting work we were doing for no reason at all.

The ROI on that one line was the best of anything I shipped that quarter, and I shipped real features that quarter. That ratio should make you a little uncomfortable. It does me.

The rule: the highest-leverage performance work is usually not making the slow thing fast. It's finding the fast thing you're doing a million times for nothing.

Go check your own hot paths

You almost certainly have one of these. Not necessarily a log line — the pattern is wider than logging:

  • Eager serialization that gets discarded — building a string/JSON for a log, a metric tag, or an error message that only matters on the unhappy path.
  • Work done before a guard instead of behind it — computing a value, then checking whether you needed it.
  • Debug conveniences that outlived the debugging — the console.log you added to find a bug in 2023 that's still running in 2026.

Find the three or four functions that run on every request. Read them not for correctness — they're correct — but for waste: what are they building that they then throw away? That's where the money is.

The rule: hot paths don't care about your intentions. They run millions of times. A "harmless" line in the wrong place is a tax you pay on every request until someone, by accident, reads the right log.

Disclosure: I build on xenition, a workspace assistant that builds and runs agents — and agents are merciless at generating exactly this kind of "correct but wasteful" code, because a clean, confident diff hides a pointless allocation just as well as it hides a logic bug. A lot of my "read hot paths for waste, not just correctness" paranoia is earned on our own systems. Read it as a builder's bias; I'd rather name it than hide it.

What's the dumbest expensive line you've ever shipped — the one that was individually correct and collectively a disaster? I'll go first in the comments, and I want the horror stories: the ones that only turned up because someone was looking for something else.

articles.title: NanoScript Update: Traversal Methods Are Finally Here!
articles.description: Hey guys! In my last post, I shared why I made NanoScript for Vlox. I wanted to avoid heavy...
articles.body_html:
Hey guys! In my last post, I shared why I made NanoScript for Vlox. I wanted to avoid heavy frameworks but also skip the long code of vanilla JavaScript. Back then, I mentioned that some features were still missing. Today, I am happy to tell you that the DOM traversal methods are finished and ready to use!

You no longer have to write complex vanilla code to move around your HTML elements.

What's New?

I wanted moving between parents, siblings, and children to feel very simple. Here are the new tools I added to NanoScript:

  • .parent() - Finds the immediate parent element.
  • .children() - Gets all the direct child elements.
  • .next() - Finds the next sibling element.
  • .prev() - Finds the previous sibling element.
  • .closest(selector) - Looks up the tree to find the nearest parent matching a specific name.

Just like the rest of NanoScript, these new methods don't take up much memory. And now, here is a quick example of how it makes your code look cleaner when you click a button to hide a card:

NS(".delete-btn").on("click", function () {
    NS(this).closest(".card").css("display", "none");
});

What's Next?

Now that traversal tools are done, I will start working on the fetch wrapper. This will help you make API network calls easily without loading external libraries like Axios. I'm also working on the official documentation, which will be ready very soon.

Try It Out!

Please try NanoScript for your next small project and let me know what you think!

You can see the source code and star the project here: https://github.com/Hfs2024/NanoScript

Leave a comment below and tell me what features you want me to build next!

articles.title: I Replaced My Entire Dev Workflow With AI Agents — Here's What Actually Worked
articles.description: I didn't set out to "replace my workflow with AI." I set out to answer a narrower, more honest...
articles.body_html:
I didn't set out to "replace my workflow with AI." I set out to answer a narrower, more honest question: which parts of my job are actually typing, and which parts are judgment I've been pretending were typing?

So I took my normal pipeline — plan, write, test, review, debug, ship — and moved each stage onto an agent, one at a time, for a few weeks. I kept whatever held and ripped out whatever didn't.

Here's the stage-by-stage result. No scorecard, no "I shipped 40 PRs" number — just the shape of what won and what quietly broke.

Stage 1: Planning — the agent is great at writing a plan, bad at having one

I expected planning to be the agent's weakest stage. It's half right.

Hand an agent a vague ticket — "users are complaining checkout is slow" — and ask for a plan, and you get something that looks like a plan: numbered steps, files to touch, a rollback note. It reads well. It is also frequently a plan for the wrong problem, because the agent filled the ambiguity with the most statistically likely interpretation, not the true one.

What actually worked was inverting it. I stopped asking the agent to decide the plan and started asking it to draft the plan from a spec I'd already pinned down. The judgment — what problem are we even solving — stayed with me. The typing — turning that into acceptance criteria, edge cases, a file list — went to the agent, and it's genuinely faster than me at that.

The rule: an agent turns a decision into a document beautifully. It cannot make the decision for you — and its confident draft will hide that it didn't.

Stage 2: Writing code — won, on exactly the work you'd expect

This is the stage everyone pictures, and it's the least interesting result because it's the one that just works.

The agent won clean on anything where the hard part was typing, not deciding:

  • CRUD endpoints with a clear schema
  • a migration with a written spec
  • wiring a form to an API I'd already designed
  • a mechanical refactor across 30 files — and crucially, it doesn't get bored on file 27, which is exactly where I introduce a typo
  • dependency bumps and the follow-on fixes

It lost on anything where the code was the easy part and the decision was buried in it: "why is this column nullable," "should this be one service or two," "is this edge case real or theoretical." The agent will answer all three confidently and sometimes wrongly, and the code it writes on top of the wrong answer is clean, tested, and shippable-looking.

The rule: agents are fastest exactly where the code is downstream of a decision you already made. The danger is they'll happily make the decision too, and you can't see that in the diff.

Stage 3: Testing — this was the real surprise, and the real trap

Writing tests is high-typing, low-glory work, so I assumed it was pure upside. It mostly is — the agent wrote months of "we'll get to it later" tests with no ego and no counter-pitch. That part was a gift.

But there's a trap underneath it that took me a week to see:

If the same agent writes the code and the tests, the tests pass — and they're worthless. They don't test whether the code is correct. They test whether the code does what the code does. The agent read its own implementation and wrote tests that encode its own assumptions, including the wrong ones. Green board, zero signal.

The fix was structural, not prompt-level: the test agent is a different agent, and it gets the spec, not the implementation. Now the tests encode what the thing is supposed to do, and when they disagree with the code, that disagreement is the whole point.

The rule: code and tests from the same agent agree with each other, not with reality. Separate the author from the examiner, or you're just asking the model to grade its own homework.

Stage 4: Review — where I learned the workflow didn't actually get shorter

Here's the stage I got wrong for the longest.

I added a reviewer agent to read every diff before I did. It's good — it catches the mechanical stuff fast: an unhandled error path, a missing null check, a test that asserts nothing. For that class of bug it's a better first pass than tired-me at 6pm.

What it cannot do is the review that actually matters: is this change solving the right problem, and does it break something three files away that isn't in the diff? That's the exact failure mode the code agent produces — every line individually correct, the decision wrong, and nothing in the diff looks wrong because nothing in the diff is wrong locally.

So the reviewer agent triages; it doesn't absolve. The judgment review still lands on me. And that's when it clicked: I hadn't removed work from my week. I'd moved it. Less time typing code, far more time writing specs up front and reading diffs like a hostile stranger wrote them.

The rule: a second agent reviewing the first agent's work catches typos, not decisions. The judgment review is not delegable, and pretending it is, is how a clean diff with a wrong decision gets merged.

Stage 5: Debugging — won when the loop was closed, lost when it needed a hunch

Debugging split cleanly.

When there's a closed feedback loop — a failing test, a stack trace, a reproducible error — the agent is excellent. It runs the test, reads the failure, forms a hypothesis, patches, re-runs. That loop is native to an agent with a terminal, and it'll grind through it faster and more patiently than I will.

When the bug needs a hunch — "it's slow but only in prod," "this only happens for users who signed up before the migration" — the agent flails. It needs the thing it doesn't have: the half-memory of a decision made eight months ago that never made it into the code. That's where a human who was there beats any amount of context window.

The rule: agents close loops; they don't form hunches. Give them the reproduction and they're great. Ask them to find the reproduction in a vague prod report and you're better off driving.

Stage 6: The boring glue — pure, unambiguous win

PR descriptions. Changelogs. Commit messages. Release notes. Backfilling docstrings. Writing the "why" comment I always skip.

This is high-typing, low-judgment, and nobody's ego is attached to it. It is the least discussed stage and the one with the cleanest return. If you're going to put one agent in your workflow tomorrow, make it this one — zero risk, immediate time back, and it quietly makes everyone else's code more readable.

The rule: the safest, highest-ROI agent is the one writing the prose around your code, not the code.

The honest summary: the bottleneck moved, it didn't disappear

If you chart my week before and after, the total didn't shrink much. What changed is where the time goes:

Stage Before After
Deciding what to build some more
Writing the spec little a lot more
Typing the code a lot little
Writing tests little (be honest) some — but reviewing them
Reviewing diffs some a lot more
The boring glue always skipped done, automatically

The agents genuinely won the typing. But every hour they gave me back on typing, they handed back as spec-writing and diff-reading — because those are the two places where their confident wrongness has to be caught by my judgment.

That's not a complaint. It's the actual job now, and it's a better job. But it's a different one, and the people getting burned are the ones who think "the AI writes the code" means "the AI does the work." The code was never the work. It was the part that happened to look like the work.

What I'd actually tell you to do

  1. Start with the glue** (Stage 6). Zero risk, instant payoff, builds your trust in the tooling.
  2. Then the high-typing code** (Stage 2) — but only where you've already made the decision. Write the spec first, by hand.
  3. Split your test agent from your code agent** (Stage 3). This is the single highest-leverage structural choice in the whole setup.
  4. Keep the judgment review on a human.** Use a reviewer agent as a first pass, never as the last word.
  5. Read every diff like a stranger wrote it** — because one did, and it's a stranger that never gets tired and never says "I'm not sure about this part."

Disclosure: I build on xenition, a workspace assistant that builds and runs agents — so I ran a lot of this on our own agents against our own backlog. Read my "always keep a skeptic on the diff" stance as a builder's bias; I'd rather name it than hide it.

If you've moved part of your workflow onto agents: which stage held, and which one quietly burned you? I'm most interested in the stage you assumed was safe and wasn't.

articles.title: Vue watch vs watchEffect: The Complete Guide
articles.description: Vue's watch() and watchEffect() look interchangeable but track dependencies, run timing, and cleanup differently. The exact rules, verified against Vue 3.5.
articles.body_html:
You type "vue" into a search box, one letter at a time. Four requests go out — for v, vu, vue, and the deleted-and-retyped vue again — and the one for v happens to come back last. The screen ends up showing results for a single letter, on top of a watch() callback that looks completely correct. Nothing in that callback is wrong. The watcher just never learned that a newer run had already made it obsolete.

This is the article that fixes that, and along the way answers the question every Vue developer eventually asks: when do I reach for watch(), when do I reach for watchEffect(), and why does my callback keep firing at the wrong moment?

What you'll learn

By the end of this article you'll be able to:

  • Explain the real difference between watch() and watchEffect() — not "one is explicit, one is automatic," but what that difference costs you
  • Pick the correct flush timing (pre, post, sync) for a watcher that needs to read the DOM
  • Use onWatcherCleanup to cancel a stale async response before it overwrites a newer one
  • Stop a watcher manually, and know when Vue stops it for you
  • Recognize the specific ways both APIs quietly track (or fail to track) the wrong things

Prerequisites

You should already be comfortable with ref(), reactive(), and computed() in the Composition API. If "why does destructuring a reactive() object lose reactivity" isn't yet second nature, read Vue Reactivity Explained: ref vs reactive first — this article assumes that mental model and builds on it.

This is written against Vue 3.5.x (verified September 2026). Version-specific notes (the once option, onWatcherCleanup) are called out where they apply.

Table of contents

  • The problem: a watcher with no memory
  • The mental model: pull vs. push tracking
  • Stage 1: the smallest watch()
  • Stage 2: the same job with watchEffect()
  • Stage 3: multiple sources, and watching inside an object
  • Stage 4: immediate, deep, and once
  • Stage 5: flush timing — pre, post, sync
  • Stage 6: cleanup and the race condition, fixed
  • Stopping a watcher
  • Edge cases and gotchas
  • Best practices
  • FAQ
  • Cheat sheet
  • Key takeaways

The problem: a watcher with no memory

Here's the search box, written the way it's tempting to write it the first time:

<script setup>
import { ref, watch } from "vue";

const query = ref("");
const results = ref([]);

watch(query, async (q) => {
  if (!q) {
    results.value = [];
    return;
  }
  const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`);
  results.value = await res.json();
});
</script>

Every keystroke fires a new request, and requests do not resolve in the order they were sent. If the request for v is slow and the request for vue is fast, vue's results land first and v's results land after, silently overwriting them. The callback did exactly what it was written to do; it just never asked "am I still the most recent run?"

That question is exactly what a watcher's cleanup mechanism answers. Getting there first requires being precise about what watch() and watchEffect() actually are.

The mental model: pull vs. push tracking

The mental model: watch() is told what to watch. watchEffect() discovers what to watch by running once and recording every reactive value it reads. Everything else — old/new values, laziness, immediacy — falls out of that one distinction.

  • watch(source, callback) takes an explicit source (a ref, a getter, a reactive() object, or an array of them) and a callback. It does not run on creation by default. It runs only when the named source changes, and it hands the callback both the new and the old value.
  • watchEffect(fn) takes a single function with no separate source. It runs immediately, once, synchronously (well — see flush timing below) to figure out what it read, and re-runs itself in full whenever any of those dependencies change. There is no "old value" concept, because there's no fixed source to diff against — the whole function reruns.

Put differently: watch is a subscription to a specific address. watchEffect is a subscription to whatever addresses this function happens to visit today — and it can visit different addresses on different runs, exactly like a computed() getter does. The dependency-tracking mechanism (a run records every reactive value it reads) is shared across computed, watch's getter-form sources, and watchEffect alike.

Stage 1: the smallest watch() 

import { ref, watch } from "vue";

const count = ref(0);

watch(count, (newVal, oldVal) => {
  console.log(`count went from ${oldVal} to ${newVal}`);
});

count.value++; // logs: "count went from 0 to 1"

Key concept: the callback did not run when watch was declared — only after count changed. That's the "lazy by default" behavior, and it's the first thing that trips people up coming from watchEffect.

Stage 2: the same job with watchEffect() 

import { ref, watchEffect } from "vue";

const count = ref(0);

watchEffect(() => {
  console.log(`count is now ${count.value}`);
});
// logs immediately: "count is now 0"

count.value++; // logs: "count is now 1"

Key concept: watchEffect ran once immediately, on creation, before anything changed — because it has to run once just to discover that count is a dependency. watch never needed to run to know its source; you named it.

If the job is "sync this state to something external, right now and on every future change" — a document title, a localStorage key, an analytics call — watchEffect is usually the shorter answer. Need the old value, or need to stay silent until one specific thing changes? Reach for watch.

Stage 3: multiple sources, and watching inside an object

watch accepts an array of sources, and hands the callback matching arrays of new/old values:

watch([firstName, lastName], ([newFirst, newLast], [oldFirst, oldLast]) => {
  console.log(`${oldFirst} ${oldLast} -> ${newFirst} ${newLast}`);
});

Watching a single property of a reactive() object requires a getter function, not the bare property — because reactive().someProp is just a plain value the instant you read it out of the object, with no reference back to the proxy:

const state = reactive({ count: 0, name: "vue" });

// Wrong: this is a snapshot number, not a reactive source.
// watch(state.count, cb) never fires.

// Correct: a getter re-reads the proxy every time Vue checks it.
watch(
  () => state.count,
  (newCount, oldCount) => console.log(newCount, oldCount)
);

This is the same "reactivity is a subscription made at read time" rule from the ref vs reactive article — watch needs something it can re-read, and a getter is how you hand it that.

Stage 4: immediate, deep, and once

Three options on watch change when and how often it fires (watchEffect accepts only flush, covered next, plus the dev-only onTrack/onTrigger — it runs on creation and tracks everything it reads, so immediate, deep and once don't apply):

watch(source, callback, {
  immediate: true, // also run once, right away, with oldValue undefined
  deep: true,      // walk the whole object/array, not just the top-level reference
  once: true,      // (Vue 3.4+) auto-stop after the callback fires the first time
});

deep: true is the one to use sparingly. Watching a getter that returns an object (() => state.someObject) or a ref holding one only fires when the whole object is replaced (a reactive() object passed directly is already implicitly deep); deep walks every nested property so a change three levels down also fires — at the cost of Vue actually traversing the structure to set that tracking up. On a large or deeply nested object, that traversal is real work.

Stage 5: flush timing — pre, post, sync

Both watch and watchEffect accept flush, and it answers a different question than the options above: relative to a component's own re-render, when does this callback run?

flush value When it runs Default?
'pre' Before the component re-renders Yes, for both APIs
'post' After the component has re-rendered and the DOM is updated No
'sync' Synchronously, the instant the dependency is written No

This connects directly to the batching behavior from Vue nextTick Explained: a pre-flush watcher (the default) can run before the DOM reflects the change that triggered it. If your callback needs to measure or read an element that just changed size or content, flush: 'pre' will read stale layout:

watch(
  items,
  () => {
    // With the default 'pre' flush, the DOM here may not yet
    // reflect the new `items` — this measurement can be one step behind.
    console.log(listRef.value.scrollHeight);
  },
  { flush: "post" } // wait for the DOM update first
);

flush: 'sync' skips Vue's batching queue entirely and runs the instant the dependency is written — useful for invalidating an external cache the moment something changes, but dangerous on sources mutated many times synchronously (e.g. an array filled in a loop), since it fires on every single mutation with no batching.

Stage 6: cleanup and the race condition, fixed

Back to the search box. The fix is to give each run a way to say "abort me if a newer run has already started" — and both watch and watchEffect give you exactly that, as onWatcherCleanup() (3.5+), which must be called synchronously during the callback (before any await):

<script setup>
import { ref, watch, onWatcherCleanup } from "vue"; // onWatcherCleanup: Vue 3.5+

const query = ref("");
const results = ref([]);

watch(query, async (q) => {
  if (!q) {
    results.value = [];
    return;
  }

  const controller = new AbortController();
  onWatcherCleanup(() => controller.abort());

  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`, {
      signal: controller.signal,
    });
    results.value = await res.json();
  } catch (e) {
    if (e.name !== "AbortError") throw e; // an aborted run is expected, not an error
  }
});
</script>

Key concept: onWatcherCleanup registers a function that Vue calls right before the next run of this same watcher — and also when the component unmounts. Type vue, and the moment the e keystroke starts a new run, the previous run's cleanup fires first, aborting its in-flight fetch. An aborted request rejects with an AbortError instead of resolving, so it can never reach results.value — and the try/catch swallows just that expected rejection, which would otherwise surface through Vue's error handler on every superseded keystroke. Order of arrival stops mattering, because only the current, un-aborted request is allowed to write.

The same mechanism is also passed as the callback's third parameter (the only option before 3.5, and still supported):

watch(query, async (q, oldQ, onCleanup) => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  onCleanup(() => controller.abort());
  // ...
});

The two forms differ here: onWatcherCleanup must be called before the first await — after it, Vue can't tell which watcher run it belongs to, so dev mode warns and the cleanup is silently dropped. The onCleanup argument is bound to its watcher, so it isn't subject to that constraint.

Stopping a watcher

Both watch and watchEffect return a handle — call it (or .stop()) to stop; since 3.5 it also has .pause() / .resume():

const stop = watchEffect(() => {
  console.log(count.value);
});

stop(); // this effect will never run again

You rarely need to call this yourself inside a component: a watcher created synchronously during setup() or <script setup> is automatically stopped when the component unmounts; one created later from an async callback (a setTimeout, a .then) inside that same <script setup> is not. You need the manual stop() mostly for watchers created outside a component's setup — inside a composable that runs after mount, in a store, or in plain JS — where Vue has no unmount to tie it to.

Edge cases and gotchas

  • await breaks dependency discovery. watchEffect only tracks reads that happen synchronously before the first await. Anything read after an await inside the function is invisible to it and will not trigger a re-run if it changes.
  • A getter that reads nothing reactive never fires. watch(() => someObj.plainProperty, cb) looks correct but never runs if plainProperty isn't itself reactive — there's nothing for Vue to subscribe to.
  • watchEffect can over-track. Because it tracks everything the function body reads, a large conditional inside it can pick up dependencies you didn't intend, causing extra re-runs. watch with an explicit source avoids this by construction.
  • .push/.splice fire a non-deep watcher only when the source is the reactive() array itself (implicitly deep). watch(itemsRef, cb) on a ref([]), or a getter like () => state.items, tracks only the array reference — in-place mutations need deep: true, or watch () => items.value.length.
  • immediate: true hands undefined as oldValue on that first synthetic run (an empty array [] when watching an array of sources) — always guard against it if the callback compares old and new.

Best practices

  • Reach for watchEffect when the job is "keep this side effect in sync with whatever it reads" and you don't need the old value — document titles, localStorage, imperative DOM syncing.
  • Reach for watch when you need the previous value, need the callback to stay silent until one specific thing changes (not everything the function happens to read), or want lazy behavior by default.
  • Default to flush: 'pre' (the default) unless the callback reads the DOM — then use 'post'. Reserve 'sync' for cache-invalidation-style work that must happen before Vue's own batching, and never on a source that's mutated many times in one tick, like an array.
  • Always pair an async watcher with cleanup the moment more than one run can be in flight at once — a search box, a resource fetched by an ID prop, anything driven by fast user input.
  • Avoid deep: true on large objects if you can watch a specific derived getter instead; the traversal cost is real.

FAQ

Does watchEffect run on component mount?

It runs when it's created — during setup(), before mount — synchronously with the default flush: 'pre'; with flush: 'post' (watchPostEffect) even the first run waits until after render. That first run is also how it discovers its dependencies.

What's the difference between watch's deep option and watchEffect?

They're unrelated axes. deep controls how far into a reactive object watch traverses to detect a change. watchEffect always tracks only what it actually reads during a run, deep or shallow, because it has no fixed source to traverse — it just doesn't re-read nested properties unless your function body does.

Why isn't my watch callback firing when I mutate a reactive object property?

The most common cause is watching a plain snapshot instead of a getter — see Stage 3. The second most common cause is watching a ref holding an object and mutating a nested property without deep: true (the object is reactive, but watch(ref) only tracks .value); the ref's own .value reference hasn't changed, so a shallow watch sees nothing.

How do I stop a watcher manually?

Call the function watch/watchEffect returns: const stop = watch(...); stop();. For a watcher created synchronously inside <script setup>, you rarely need to — unmount does it for you.

Is watchEffect the same as a computed?

No. computed() returns a cached value meant to be read elsewhere and must stay pure (no side effects). watchEffect runs a side effect and returns nothing meant to be read — it's for doing something, not deriving something.

Does watch support async callbacks?

Yes — async (newVal, oldVal) => { ... } works exactly as shown above. Just remember that oldVal and newVal are captured before the await, and that any onWatcherCleanup() call must happen before the first await.

Cheat sheet 

import { ref, reactive, watch, watchEffect, onWatcherCleanup } from "vue";

// watch(): explicit source, lazy by default, gives old + new value
watch(source, (newVal, oldVal) => { /* ... */ });
watch([a, b], ([newA, newB], [oldA, oldB]) => { /* ... */ });
watch(() => reactiveObj.prop, (newVal, oldVal) => { /* ... */ }); // getter for a nested property

// watchEffect(): auto-tracked, runs immediately, no old value
watchEffect(() => { document.title = title.value; });

// Options (watch only, except flush which both accept)
watch(source, cb, {
  immediate: true, // also run once immediately (oldValue is undefined that time)
  deep: true,      // traverse nested properties, not just the top reference
  once: true,      // Vue 3.4+: auto-stop after first fire
  flush: "post",   // 'pre' (default) | 'post' (after DOM update) | 'sync' (no batching)
});

// Cleanup: cancel a stale async run before the next one starts (Vue 3.5+)
watch(source, async (val) => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  onWatcherCleanup(() => controller.abort()); // before the first await
  try {
    await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
  } catch (e) {
    if (e.name !== "AbortError") throw e;
  }
});

// Stopping
const stop = watchEffect(() => { /* ... */ });
stop(); // manual — usually unnecessary for watchers created synchronously in <script setup>, which auto-stop on unmount
// Vue 3.5+: the handle also has stop.pause() / stop.resume()

Key takeaways

  • watch is told its source explicitly and is lazy by default; watchEffect discovers its sources by running once, immediately, and re-runs the whole function when any of them change.
  • flush decides when relative to the DOM update — 'pre' (default) can run before a DOM change, 'post' waits for it, 'sync' skips batching entirely.
  • onWatcherCleanup (Vue 3.5+) — or the callback's third onCleanup argument, the only option on earlier versions — fires right before the next run, which is exactly what stops a slow, stale async response from overwriting a fresher one.
  • A watcher created synchronously in <script setup> stops itself on unmount; one created outside a component's setup needs its returned stop() called by hand.

The search box from the top of this article isn't really a search-box bug — it's what happens any time a watcher's previous run outlives its next run and nobody told it to stop. Once cleanup is a habit rather than an afterthought, that entire category of bug stops happening. What's the last race condition you tracked down that turned out to be a missing cleanup?
