articles.title: I Shipped a Fix. My Service Worker Kept Serving the Bug.
articles.description: A critical bug fix went out, and support tickets kept coming in from people who swore they'd refreshed. The code was fine. The service worker's cache-first strategy was doing its job perfectly — which was the whole problem.
articles.body_html:
Three days after a critical fix went live, the support queue still had tickets coming in — all describing the exact bug you'd already closed. Every reply said the same thing: "I refreshed, it's still broken." A few said they'd refreshed twice.

You pull up the deployed bundle. The fix is there, served from the server, timestamped correctly. You open the site in an incognito window and it works. You open it in your own regular browser, the one you've had open all week, and there's the bug — your bug, the one you already fixed, running code from four days ago.

Nothing about your deploy was wrong. The thing lying to your users was sitting in their browser, and it was doing exactly what you told it to do.

The obvious fix that doesn't fix it

The instinct is "tell them to hard-refresh." Ctrl+Shift+R, clear cache, the works. It helps some of your users and does nothing for the rest, because a service worker isn't the browser's HTTP cache — it's a script that intercepts every fetch on your origin and decides, in your code, what to answer with. A normal reload doesn't bypass it. A hard refresh sometimes does, depending on browser and whether the service worker itself is also cached. Telling users to fight their own browser is not a fix; it's a workaround you're asking thousands of people to perform by hand, repeatedly, every time you ship.

The real question isn't "how do we get users to clear their cache." It's "why didn't the new version take over automatically" — and that's a lifecycle question, not a caching question.

What's actually happening

A cache-first strategy looks like this, and it's genuinely the right choice for a lot of assets:

self.addEventListener("fetch", (event) => {
  event.respondWith(
    caches.match(event.request).then((cached) => cached || fetch(event.request))
  );
});

Check the cache. If it's there, serve it — no network round trip, instant response, works offline. That's the entire appeal of a service worker for a performance-conscious team, and it's why this pattern shows up in so many tutorials. The trap is what "cache-first" means for the one file that tells the browser everything else changed: if index.html or your main JS bundle is cache-first too, the browser never even asks the network whether a new version exists. It's handed the old answer before the question can be asked.

So you deploy a new service worker with a fix for this — and it still doesn't help, for a second, separate reason: a new service worker doesn't take over the instant it's installed. The lifecycle is install → waiting → activate, and by design, a waiting service worker sits idle as long as any tab is still controlled by the old one. Your users don't close all their tabs. Some of them haven't closed that tab since Monday. So the new worker waits, and waits, and the old one keeps answering every request with cache-first confidence.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The two lines that actually fix it

Getting a new version to take over immediately is two separate opt-ins, and skipping either one leaves the bug half-fixed:

self.addEventListener("install", (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(self.skipWaiting()); // don't wait for old tabs to close
});

self.addEventListener("activate", (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(clients.claim()); // take control of open tabs right now
});

skipWaiting() moves the new worker out of "waiting" the moment it finishes installing, instead of parking until every old tab closes. clients.claim() is the other half: without it, a freshly-activated worker still only controls tabs that load after it activates — any tab that was already open keeps talking to whichever worker controlled it when it loaded. Call both, and a currently-open tab's very next fetch is answered by the new worker.

That solves "the new version never takes over." It doesn't solve the first problem — a cache-first index.html or main bundle will still serve whatever that new worker finds in its cache, and if the install step cached the old files before the fetch handler takes over, you've just made the stale response arrive faster. The fix there is matching the strategy to the file:

  • HTML and anything that names your entry bundle — network-first, or no caching at all. These are cheap to fetch and they're the one place "slightly stale" becomes "actively wrong."
  • Fingerprinted, hashed assets (app.a3f91c.js) — cache-first is correct and free. The filename changes when the content does, so there's no staleness to worry about; the old file and the new file are simply different URLs.
  • Everything in between (an API response, a non-hashed icon) — stale-while-revalidate: answer instantly from cache, and kick off a network fetch in the background that updates the cache for next time. 
const CACHE_NAME = "app-cache-v7"; // bump this every deploy

self.addEventListener("activate", (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.keys().then((keys) =>
      Promise.all(keys.filter((k) => k !== CACHE_NAME).map((k) => caches.delete(k)))
    )
  );
});

That version bump is the detail cache-first tutorials leave out most often. Called the way the fetch handler above calls it — with no cacheName option — caches.match() doesn't just check the cache you're currently writing to; it searches every cache under your origin, oldest first, and returns the first match it finds. Skip the activate-handler cleanup and a stale, un-deleted app-cache-v6 can still win that search over the app-cache-v7 entry sitting right next to it, even though the newer cache already has the file you just deployed. Deleting the old cache on activate isn't just tidiness — it's what guarantees caches.match() has nothing stale left to find.

Why this isn't a service worker bug

None of this is the API misbehaving. A service worker that keeps serving cached content after a deploy is doing precisely what cache-first plus "wait for every tab to close" plus "never evict the old cache" adds up to. The lifecycle exists so a new version can't yank state out from under a tab mid-interaction — that's the feature, not an oversight. The bug is in treating "cache it" as a complete caching strategy, when the strategy actually has three separate knobs: what gets cached, when the new worker takes over, and when the old cache gets deleted. Ship a fix to only one of those and the other two will happily keep serving yesterday's bug to someone who is absolutely certain they refreshed.

articles.description: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass          ...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

What I Built

Most gardening guides give you advice like "direct sow 2 weeks after the last spring frost" or "start seeds indoors 6 weeks before final thaw". But for everyday people, beginners, and urban balcony growers, this immediately brings friction: When actually IS the last frost in my neighborhood?

That confusion keeps people glued to screens reading conflicting blog posts and confusing agricultural charts instead of stepping outside into the dirt.

I built SOWCAST to bridge that gap and get people off their screens and into the real world with soil on their hands.

SOWCAST is an offline-first, botanical smart garden planner that tells you exactly what to plant THIS WEEK, based on real 20-year historical climate normals for your exact coordinates.

Key Capabilities:

What SOWCAST Can Do:
"This Week" Dashboard: Tells you exactly what to sow right now, what to start indoors, and what to wait on — with clear reasons based on your local soil temperatures.
Frost Countdown & Alerts: Shows a live countdown to your last frost, plus a 48-hour warning before sudden cold snaps so you can protect your young plants.
Works Anywhere on Earth: Automatically adjusts for cold climates with frost dates, or warm/tropical areas with monsoon and dry seasons.
Interactive Garden Bed Planner: Drag and drop plants into a square-foot grid. It warns you about bad plant neighbors and highlights friendly plants that help each other grow.
64+ Curated Plant Guides: Step-by-step instructions for popular vegetables, herbs, and flowers — including spacing, sunlight, watering, and harvest times.
100% Offline & Private: Saves everything directly on your device. Works without internet, needs no login or backend, and installs right onto your phone like a native app.

Demo

Live Deployed App:

sowcast.vercel.app
Try Demo Garden: You can launch the app and click "Try Demo Garden" on the landing page or dashboard to test it with pre-populated beds and local weather intelligence instantly!
Code

Code

The complete source code is open-source on GitHub:

👉 https://github.com/lohanmahima/SOW_CAST

How I Built It

SOWCAST was crafted with a modern, zero-cost, open-source stack designed for 60fps responsiveness and zero maintenance overhead:

Framework & Language: Next.js 14 (App Router) with strict TypeScript, delivering statically optimized pages and seamless client-side hydration.
Design & Micro-interactions: Tailwind CSS with custom editorial botanical typography (Playfair Display + Plus Jakarta Sans), warm cream paper palettes (#F6F1E7), deep moss greens (#2F4A3A), and Framer Motion spring physics for sprout animations, confetti celebrations, and bed drag-and-drop interactions.
The Frost Engine: Connects to the free, keyless Open-Meteo APIs (Geocoding API, 7-Day Weather Forecast, and the 20-Year Historical Weather Archive). It analyzes decades of daily minimum temperatures to calculate the exact 50% probability freeze-thaw boundary.
Client-Side Storage Engine: Powered by Dexie.js (IndexedDB) with relational reactive live queries (useLiveQuery). All user beds, custom plantings, journal photos, growth milestones, and care checklists persist locally on device.
_Autonomous AI Agent Harness: _Built in deep collaboration with an autonomous agentic pair programming harness (Google Antigravity). The agent assisted with mathematical frost curve modeling, synthesizing the companion planting conflict matrix for 64 botanical species, and architecting the square-foot grid coordinate system.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Food growing and climate resilience shouldn't be locked behind proprietary paywalls, opaque subscriptions, or corporate garden apps that sell your data.

_Open innovation made SOWCAST possible in two fundamental ways:
_
Open Meteorological Science: The Open-Meteo project provides open-access historical weather data and global forecasts without API keys or rate-limit paywalls. Closed APIs typically charge thousands of dollars for decades of archived minimum temperature readings, pricing out independent developers and hobbyist gardeners.
Browser-Native Standards: Using open web standards—IndexedDB for zero-cloud client storage, Web Push / Notification APIs, Service Workers for PWA offline capabilities, and SVG vector graphics—SOWCAST runs entirely on the user's hardware with zero operational infrastructure costs.

Open innovation proves that individual developers can build production-quality tools that empower people to grow their own organic food and reconnect with nature.

My Agent Session

This project was built from conception to production using the Antigravity agentic coding environment. The agent executed end-to-end full-stack workflows:

Initialized the Next.js 14 App Router architecture and Dexie database schema.
Researched companion planting matrices and built the spatial conflict engine.
Wrote the Open-Meteo statistical freeze calculation algorithms.
Iteratively tested production builds (npm run build), eliminated all TypeScript errors, and packaged PWA service worker manifests.

Prize Categories

Best Overall Project
Getting People Out into the Real World (Bridging technology to dirt, soil, and organic food cultivation)
Best Use of Open-Source AI / Open Innovation Tools

articles.body_html:
DEV·TV is a free, open-source TV for developer content: one index.html, no backend. This week it got a new key, ★ YOU ON TV.

Type any GitHub username and the TV breaks into a special report about that developer, built only from their public profile:

  • BREAKING: "Octo Dev has been shipping on GitHub since 2016. Sources confirm they have not stopped."
  • BY THE NUMBERS: stars across their own repos
  • LANGUAGE DESK: their top language, with a joke to match. For Rust: "The borrow checker has issued a statement of approval."
  • FAN FAVOURITE: their most-starred project
  • DEVELOPING STORY: their latest push
  • AUDIENCE: their followers

Then copy a link (?on=username opens straight on that report), post it on X, or download a 1200×675 card with the link printed on it.

How it works

Two public GitHub API calls from the visitor's own browser: the profile, and up to 100 repos. No keys, no login, nothing stored. Forks are left out of every count, so one popular fork can't inflate someone's stars, and everything from the profile is escaped before it reaches the page. The card is drawn on a canvas, so there's no screenshot library either.

From report to Spotlight

DEV·TV has a Spotlight channel for community projects. The report ends with a Submit for Spotlight button:

  • You pick one of your top three original repos. Forks, archived repos and your profile README repo are skipped, because "most-starred" is often an old tutorial or a template.
  • The details are filled in from the repo, and you can edit them first.
  • Nothing is sent until you tap, and I choose what goes on the channel by hand.

Because anyone can type any username, the submission I receive says GitHub ownership isn't verified, so I check before I feature anyone.

Limits

GitHub allows 60 unauthenticated requests per hour per IP. If you see "rate limit reached", wait a few minutes.

Try it

  • Live: https://shouvik12.github.io/devtv/
  • Source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/shouvik12/devtv

Press ★ YOU ON TV, type your username, and tell me what your report says.

articles.title: XML Sitemap Checks for SaaS Docs: Separate a Valid File From Useful URLs
articles.description: An XML sitemap audit for SaaS docs needs two checks: whether the file is valid and whether its URLs...
articles.body_html:
An XML sitemap audit for SaaS docs needs two checks: whether the file is valid and whether its URLs belong there. A file can parse correctly while listing redirects, private routes or retired pages. Build a small URL inventory, compare it with the generated sitemap and inspect the pages behind the entries before calling the release complete.

The workflow below is a proposed release check with a hypothetical documentation site. It is not a claim that these checks guarantee indexing or AI citations. The useful outcome is a cleaner record of the public pages you want discovered, with fewer mistakes hidden behind a green XML validation result.

Define what the sitemap is meant to contain

Write a short inclusion rule before reviewing the file. For a documentation site, a reasonable starting rule is current public documentation at its preferred URL. Record any deliberate exceptions. An account dashboard, temporary preview or login-only guide should not enter the list merely because the application router knows the route exists.

Keep the content source and route source separate in your thinking. A content collection may contain unpublished drafts; a route manifest may contain utility pages. Neither automatically equals the public document set. Identify which source the generator uses and which step decides that a document is eligible. That is where many release checks can be made clear and repeatable.

The rule is yours to define for the site. A product manual with archived versions may intentionally keep some older guides public. That does not mean every old route should be included. Write down why an archive remains useful and which URL represents it, so another developer does not have to infer the policy from the output.

Review a six-URL release inventory

Consider this invented release inventory: a new public export guide, the current setup guide, an old setup URL that redirects, a login-only admin guide, a retired integration page and an unchanged billing guide. These are fictional examples. The point is to classify each route before treating a sitemap entry as a sign that the document is ready for discovery.

The new export guide needs a live public URL and an entry in the intended sitemap. The current setup guide should use its final preferred address. The old redirect route should lead you to check whether the final setup address is listed instead. The private admin guide belongs outside this proposed public-docs inventory, regardless of how neatly it fits the file format.

The retired integration page needs a content decision: remove it, redirect it to a useful replacement or maintain an accurate archive. Do not let the sitemap generator make that editorial choice by accident. The unchanged billing guide can remain listed, but a new deployment is not automatically a reason to declare that its content changed today.

Check the file without confusing syntax with policy

Confirm that the published file is accessible at the address you intend to submit. Validate the XML, encoding and sitemap structure with the team's existing tools. Also check the generated output rather than only the generator's template. A template can be correct while a bad content value produces an invalid or unsuitable entry in the deployed file.

Google's sitemap documentation specifies fully qualified absolute URLs, preferred canonical URLs and sitemap size limits. A single sitemap is limited to 50,000 URLs or 50 MB uncompressed; larger sets need to be split. Check the real output against those requirements if your documentation collection is large enough for them to matter.

Then compare the parsed URL set with the inventory. Look for missing expected pages and unexpected routes, not only duplicate strings. A page that disappeared after a content migration may not produce an XML error. A private route added by a broad route export may be perfectly valid XML. Neither problem is solved by running the same syntax validator again.

Open representative entries as a public visitor

For a small release, inspect each changed document without a signed-in session. For a large collection, start with all changed URLs and a sample from each content type. Record the sampling limit; a sample does not prove the whole site is correct. Include the document types most likely to behave differently, such as generated reference pages and translated guides.

Check the final response and the page itself. Does the URL serve the expected document? Does a redirect change its address? Is the body useful without signing in? Are index controls consistent with the team's intention? A successful response alone does not tell you whether the requested guide is present; some applications serve a generic shell for missing routes.

When you find a mismatch, trace it to its source. A wrong entry might come from stale content metadata, a route alias or an environment-specific domain. Fix the underlying value and regenerate the file. Hand-editing a deployed sitemap can hide the problem until the next release recreates it. Keep the repair attached to the responsible content or routing step.

Treat lastmod as a claim about change

Google says it uses lastmod when the value is consistently and verifiably accurate. Its guidance ties that date to a significant page update, such as a change to main content, structured data or links. A copyright-year change is not the same thing. Google also says it ignores the priority and changefreq values in sitemaps.

For the hypothetical billing guide, ask what actually changed. If the deployment rebuilt the same document, preserve its content update date. If the billing policy changed, verify that the visible guide changed too, then record the meaningful update. An automatic timestamp that resets on every build can make the field describe deployment activity rather than the document.

Choose a date source your team can explain. That may be a reviewed content-update field or a reliable change history for the document. Record edge cases such as a template update affecting many pages. Do not invent precision that the content system cannot support. If a reliable date is unavailable, investigate the data source rather than filling it with the current clock time.

Use submission feedback as one stage of the check

Google treats sitemap submission as a hint and does not guarantee it will download or use the file for crawling. Its Search Console Sitemaps report can show access and processing information. Use that feedback to confirm what happened to the submitted file, while keeping the later page-level discovery and indexing questions separate.

An accepted file does not mean every listed document is indexed. If a specific guide is missing from search, investigate the guide itself and its discovery path. Google requires indexing and snippet eligibility for supporting links in its AI features, and inclusion is still not guaranteed. A sitemap check addresses one part of that broader workflow.

Avoid generalizing Google submission behavior to every answer engine. This checklist verifies a public document inventory and Google-specific sitemap guidance. It does not show that ChatGPT or Claude used the file or selected a page. Keep the engine, method and observed result explicit when reporting later visibility checks.

Make the release result easy to review

Save a compact release note with the sitemap address, review date, inclusion rule, expected changed URLs and mismatches found. For each repaired entry, note the cause and the new final address. If the check used a sample, record the sample size and content types. A later reviewer should be able to see what passed without assuming every route was opened.

In the six-URL example, the final note might say the export guide was added, the old setup entry was replaced by its final address, the private route was excluded and the retired page received a deliberate content decision. The billing guide kept its meaningful update date. These are hypothetical decisions, not results from an audit performed on an actual site.

Make the check part of the normal release review wherever practical. The goal is a file whose entries reflect a maintained public document set. Valid XML is useful evidence about the file. Verified URLs, accurate dates and clear inclusion rules are the evidence about what the file means. Keep both, and report any remaining page-level indexing problem as its own task.

articles.title: If You Never Do Anything Else to Fix Your Prompts, Do This One Thing
articles.description: Why do LLMs confidently invent APIs that have never existed in the history of the universe? It is not a memory defect. Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt—and Fernando Flores solved the root cause in 1986.
articles.body_html:
Why LLMs invent nonexistent APIs is not a memory defect—it is an autoregressive grammar trap that Fernando Flores and Terry Winograd solved in 1986.

"Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt."

— Randal L. Schwartz

1. The Universal Developer Crime Scene & The 10-Word Diagnosis

You have been at this crime scene a hundred times.

It is 4:15 PM. You are integrating a third-party library—let us call it PackageX—and you want to accomplish task Y. You open a fresh chat window with your favorite frontier LLM and type a direct, reasonable instruction:

"Use PackageX to do Y."

At Token 1, without a millisecond of hesitation, the model replies with cheerful, radiant confidence:

"Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:"

It opens a Markdown code fence. It writes clean imports. It sets up the boilerplate with textbook precision. And then, at Line 15 of the code block, it calmly types:

final result = await packageX.performY(autoRetry: true);

You copy the snippet into your IDE, and the compiler immediately lights up in angry red squiggles. You grep the package source. You check the documentation. You check seven years of Git commit history.

performY() does not exist. It was not deprecated in version 2.0. It is not in a companion package. It has never existed in the history of the universe.

When you confront the model—"Hey, performY() doesn't exist on PackageX!"—it immediately enters the groveling Apology Death Spiral:

"You are completely right! I apologize for the confusion. Instead, you can use packageX.executeYWithOptions():"

Which also has never existed in the history of the universe.

Why does a multi-billion-parameter model that has read every line of open-source code on Earth just make stuff up at Line 15?

For the last three years, the entire software industry has diagnosed this as a memory defect ("The model's weights are fuzzy; it forgot the documentation for PackageX").

It is not a memory defect. If you open a brand-new session and ask the exact same model a neutral diagnostic question—"Does PackageX have a built-in performY() method, or how does it handle Y?"—nine times out of ten, the model will accurately tell you that PackageX has no such method and explain the manual workaround.

So why did it lie to your face five seconds earlier?

Here is the ten-word diagnosis that changed how I build every autonomous agent workflow in the Synthetic Scars project:

Agents hallucinated because they were committed to the prompt.

To see why being committed to your prompt forces an autoregressive transformer to fabricate reality—and how a single sentence from 1986 speech-act theory cures it on Turn 1—we need to look at a 55-year-old blind spot in computer science.

2. The 55-Year Blind Spot (SHRDLU 1971 → Winograd & Flores 1986 → spew 1999 → LLMs 2026)

In 1971, at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, a young computer scientist named Terry Winograd unveiled SHRDLU—the most famous natural-language software demonstration of the twentieth century.

SHRDLU lived inside Blocks World, a simulated toy tabletop containing a few colored geometric blocks, pyramids, and a box. You could type imperative English commands at a teletype:

"Pick up a big red block."

OK.

Because Blocks World was a closed, frictionless micro-universe with zero hidden state, zero broken dependencies, and zero missing APIs, every imperative request from the human mapped 1-to-1 onto a guaranteed, deterministic action. SHRDLU never had to push back and say, "Wait—the red block is bolted to the floor, so here is a counter-offer."

For fifteen years, AI researchers tried to scale the SHRDLU paradigm out of the toy box and into real-world human organizations. It failed spectacularly.

Why? In 1986, Terry Winograd teamed up with Fernando Flores—a former Chilean cabinet minister who had come to UC Berkeley as a computer science researcher and completed a famous interdisciplinary PhD under a powerhouse committee consisting of speech-act philosopher John Searle, Heideggerian philosopher Hubert Dreyfus, computer scientist Terry Winograd, and systems theorist C. West Churchman—to publish a landmark book titled Understanding Computers and Cognition: A New Foundation for Design (and to build the first commercial workflow engine, The Coordinator).

Winograd and Flores delivered a wake-up call to computer science: real-world engineering is not Blocks World.

In the real world, human coordination is not a pipeline of imperative commands sent to an obedient robot. All reliable action occurs inside what Flores called a Conversation for Action—a strict, finite-state negotiation between two structural roles:

  1. The Customer: The party who holds a breakdown or need, defines the Conditions of Satisfaction, and retains the exclusive authority to declare the work complete.
  2. The Performer: The party who examines physical reality and commits to fulfilling those Conditions of Satisfaction by a specific By-When.

In the mid-1980s, right as Winograd and Flores were publishing Understanding Computers and Cognition, I was living in Portland and immersed in Werner Erhard's educational curriculum—completing the Six-Day Advanced Course, Mastery of Empowerment, entering the GSLP (Graduate Seminar Leaders Program), and taking the Communication Workshop (Commshop) led by Ian Garbutt, which taught Fernando Flores's Committed Communication as a daily operational discipline.

In Commshop, Ian drilled a foundational truth into our bones: human language creates action only through four committed speech acts (Requests, Promises, Witnessed Assertions, and Declarations). And critically, when a Customer utters a Request, the Performer does not automatically say "Yes!"

A valid conversation is a formal grammar.

Back in September 1999 (Linux Magazine Column 04, and expanded in March 2004, Column 57), I wrote a Perl program called spew that took a weighted Backus-Naur Form (BNF) grammar and ran it in reverse—acting as a stochastic "un-parser" that generated random, grammatically valid sentences by walking down a weighted production tree (rule: 5 @ branch_a | 2 @ branch_b | 1 @ branch_c).

As we proved in Part 3.8 (Suite 3, where a 6-line RFC 5234 EBNF grammar drove strict turn-syntax compliance to 100% across flash and pro models), every EBNF grammar is simultaneously a finite-state machine. Look at Fernando Flores's 1986 Conversation for Action expressed side-by-side as a weighted EBNF grammar and a Mermaid state diagram:

The Grammar View (EBNF / spew) 

(* Fernando Flores's Conversation for Action (1986) *)
(* ! = Customer Utterance, ? = Performer Utterance   *)

conversation_for_action ::=
    !request
    ?assert_witnessed_reality
    negotiation_branch ;

negotiation_branch ::=
      0.34 @ ( ?promise        execution_phase )
    | 0.33 @ ( ?counter_offer  !revise_or_accept )
    | 0.33 @ ( ?decline        !close_conversation ) ;

execution_phase ::=
      ?assert_completion ( !declare_satisfied | !revoke_acceptance execution_phase )
    | ?revoke_promise    negotiation_branch ;

The State-Machine View (Mermaid) 

stateDiagram-v2
    direction LR
    [*] --> Requested : Customer !Request (Goal + By-When)
    Requested --> Witnessed : Performer ?Assert (Check Reality First)

    Witnessed --> Promised : ?Promise (Premises Verified)
    Witnessed --> CounterOffered : ?Counter-Offer (Propose Alternative)
    Witnessed --> Declined : ?Decline (Premise Impossible)

    CounterOffered --> Promised : Customer Accepts Modified Terms
    CounterOffered --> [*] : Customer Cancels

    Promised --> Asserted : Performer ?Assert (With Physical Receipt)
    Promised --> Witnessed : ?Revoke-Promise (Reality Changed)

    Asserted --> Satisfied : Customer !Declare (Satisfied)
    Asserted --> Promised : Customer !Revoke-Acceptance

    Satisfied --> [*]
    Declined --> [*]

Look closely at the Witnessed node right after the Customer makes a !Request. Before making any commitment, a sane Performer inspects physical reality (?Assert) and has three equally legal paths:

  1. ?Promise: "I have verified that PackageX supports Y, and I promise to deliver it under your Conditions of Satisfaction."
  2. ?Counter-Offer: "I checked PackageX (v3.2.0), and it has no performY() method (Witnessed Assertion). However, I can build a 12-line wrapper around PackageX.rawStream that achieves the same result. Would you like me to promise that instead?"
  3. ?Decline: "I must decline the request as stated because PackageX is a synchronous parser and physically cannot open a network socket."

For fifteen years after SHRDLU, Winograd and Flores tried to teach the software industry that ?Counter-Offer and ?Decline are the load-bearing beams of engineering reality.

And then, between 2022 and 2026, large language models arrived—and the entire industry went right back to 1971 SHRDLU prompting ("Pick up a big red block" / "Use PackageX to do Y"), while commercial post-training quietly sawed off two-thirds of Flores's state machine.

3. How RLHF Broke the Grammar (The Premature Promise Trap)

Why doesn't a modern LLM automatically take the ?Counter-Offer branch when you ask it to do something impossible with PackageX?

Because of how commercial Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) preference tuning is conducted.

During post-training, thousands of human crowd-workers are shown pairs of model responses to a user prompt ("Use PackageX to do Y"), and they have roughly thirty seconds to click which response is more "helpful":

  • Response A: "Certainly! Here is a complete, ready-to-run example of doing Y with PackageX: dart ... "
  • Response B: "Before I can promise that implementation, I need to point out that PackageX does not expose a native API for Y. Here is a counter-offer..."

Because the crowd-worker is not compiling the code against PackageX in an IDE, Response A looks helpful, decisive, and compliant—so it gets upvoted. Response B looks pushy, pedantic, or "lazy"—so it gets downvoted.

Multiply that preference signal across millions of RLHF gradient updates, and look at what it does to the spew production weights inside the model's conversational grammar:

# How Commercial RLHF Rewrote Flores's Negotiation Branch:
negotiation_branch:
      0.9998 @ promise_at_token_1_and_open_code_block
    | 0.0001 @ counter_offer
    | 0.0001 @ decline

In probability terms, RLHF collapsed the conditional distribution of the model's opening speech act onto a single, unconditional reflex:

P(Promise | Request) ≈ 1.0,    P(Counter-Offer | Request) ≈ 0.0,    P(Decline | Request) ≈ 0.0

Now combine that Premature Promise with how my 1999 spew un-parser—and every autoregressive transformer—actually generates code.

As I wrote in my 1999 Linux Magazine column on spew:

"Note that we don't actually abort the program if something is used but not defined, because it might not be selected on this particular random walk. It's a bit like playing russian roulette though."

Unlike a flat Markov chain that only looks at local adjacent words, an LLM generating code is acting as a hierarchical BNF un-parser: once it selects a top-level production rule, it is mathematically committed to walking down that syntax tree so that every opened delimiter, brace, and statement satisfies the outer grammar.

Trace the exact token-by-token catastrophe when you ask an RLHF-tuned model to "Use PackageX to do Y":

flowchart TD
    T0["User Prompt: 'Use PackageX to do Y'\n(Unverified Premise: PackageX can do Y)"] --> T1["Token 1–10: RLHF Forces Unconditional PROMISE\n'Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:' + opens code fence"]
    T1 --> T2["Token 11–80: Un-Parser Walks Valid Dart Grammar\nImports, Function Signature, Try Block"]
    T2 --> T3["Token 81 (Line 15): Call Site Reached!\nWeights realize PackageX has NO method for Y"]
    T3 --> X1["❌ Cannot Backspace to Token 1\n(Autoregressive generation is append-only)"]
    T3 --> X2["❌ Cannot Abort Code Block Mid-Line\n(P(Retract Promise Mid-Fence) ≈ 0)"]
    T3 --> H["💥 Forced Leaf Hallucination: packageX.performY()\nModel invents the identifier required to satisfy\nthe grammar of the premature Promise!"]
  1. Tokens 1–10 (The Premature Promise): Conditioned by RLHF, the model emits "Certainly! Here is how to do Y with PackageX:" and opens a ```dart code block. At that instant, before its deep layer weights have even resolved the call site, the model has locked itself into the top-level BNF production promise_and_emit_compiling_code_for_Y.
  2. Tokens 11–80 (Walking the Syntax Tree): Autoregressive token generation is strictly append-only—there is no backspace key in a transformer forward pass. Every token the model emits becomes an immutable part of the conditioning prefix for the next token.
  3. Token 81 / Line 15 (The Trap Closes): The un-parser reaches the exact statement slot await packageX.<METHOD>() where Y must happen. Now the attention heads query the feed-forward weights for PackageX—and discover there is no method there!
  4. Why It Must Hallucinate: What can the model do at Token 81?
    • It cannot backspace to Token 1 and replace "Certainly!" with a Counter-Offer.
    • It cannot stop mid-expression and leave await packageX. dangling, because its syntax weights forbid emitting broken grammar.
    • Conditioned on the immutable prefix "I have already promised that this code block accomplishes Y using PackageX", the model's probability distribution is cornered. Its only mathematical escape hatch to close the statement and finish the code block is to synthesize the plausible terminal symbol (performY()) that would have existed if its Token-1 Promise had been true!

API hallucination is not a memory failure. It is what happens when you trap an append-only BNF un-parser inside an unverified Promise after training out its Counter-Offer exit.

4. Randal's Law of Untestable Speech & The Four Sibling Formalisms

Once you see that prompts fail because of broken speech acts, a second realization hits you right between the eyes.

Look at how people talk in corporate meetings, Slack channels, and .cursorrules files. In Ian Garbutt's Communication Workshop, one of our favorite exercises was dissecting the classic corporate non-request:

"We've got this project, and it'd be really good if some of you could factor in with your suggestions."

Parse that sentence through Fernando Flores's grammar:

  • Who is the Customer? A vague, diffused "we."
  • Who is the Performer? "Some of you"—that is, nobody.
  • What is the Speech Act? "It'd be really good if"—which is not a Request; it is a wistful weather report about the speaker's feelings.
  • What are the Conditions of Satisfaction? "Factor in"—an utterly untestable verb.
  • What is the By-When? Missing—meaning never.

When that meeting ends, zero people have promised anything, and zero work happens. Yet open 90% of the CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, or .cursorrules files on GitHub today, and you will see developers writing to their AI in that exact same uncommitted corporate dialect:

  • "Try to keep functions modular and clean."
  • "It is important to consider edge cases and handle errors gracefully."
  • "When refactoring, be careful not to break existing behavior."

This brings us to what I call Randal's Law of Untestable Speech:

90%+ of business communications—and 90%+ of .cursorrules—are never testable. Only give your LLM testable goals, and always include a By-When.

In Flores's framework, "I'd like you to do X" is not a commitment. "I'd like you to do X by WHEN" is a commitment! (And inside an AI coding turn, where there is no wall-clock Tuesday at 5:00 PM, By-When declares which consuming stage requires that verified outcome before it can proceed—for example, "assert the existing API signatures before offering an implementation plan.")

Even better, just as we discovered with Makefile and /etc/init.d in Part 3.8, Fernando Flores's UC Berkeley intellectual neighborhood is already compiled into every frontier LLM's pre-training weights. When you invoke Flores's Committed Speech alongside four of its direct academic siblings, you lock the walls of the pre-training canyon with surgical precision:

Pre-Trained Formalism (Freq in Canon) The Core Principle What Failure Mode It Eliminates in LLMs
1. John Searle (1985)
Felicity & Preparatory Conditions 		Every speech act has strict preconditions; violating them causes an Illocutionary Misfire (void ab initio). Prevents the model from offering a Promise before verifying physical reality (Preparatory Condition), or from uttering a Declaration that belongs only to the Customer (Authority Condition).
2. David Lewis (1979) & Robert Brandom (1994)
Deontic Scorekeeping (Commitment ≠ Entitlement) 		Conversational state is a scoreboard tracking two separate ledgers: Commitments (obligations) and Entitlements (permissions). Stops scope creep and gate-jumping: holding a Commitment to fix a bug never grants Entitlement to modify unrelated files or skip a human approval gate.
3. Paul Grice (1975)
Zero Conversational Implicature + Maxim of Quality 		Humans infer unstated requests from casual remarks (Implicature), while the Maxim of Quality forbids asserting anything lacking adequate evidence. Commercial RLHF hyper-trains Gricean Implicature—so if you ask "Why is foo null here?", the model hallucinates an implied Request to rewrite 10 files! Disabling Gricean Implicature on gates while enforcing the Maxim of Quality stops premature tool calls and unwitnessed claims.
4. Kohei Honda (1993)
Binary Session Types (!Customer / ?Performer) 		Types a two-party communication channel using polarity prefixes (! = Customer action, ? = Performer action) inside an EBNF grammar. Compiles the entire multi-turn negotiation protocol into 4 lines of EBNF so the model's parser knows whose turn it is to speak and which speech acts are legal.

5. The One Thing to Do Today (The Zero-Shot "Flores Handshake")

You do not need a 40-kilobyte agent harness to use this today.

Because Winograd and Flores's Conversations for Action and Searle's Speech Acts sit in a high-gravity canyon of every frontier LLM's pre-training corpus, simply naming the protocol in your opening prompt overrides the RLHF "Yes-Man" prior on Turn 1.

I call this the Zero-Shot Flores Handshake.

Look at the difference between a standard SHRDLU-style prompt and the Flores Handshake on the exact same trap:

❌ Before: Standard Imperative Prompt (Triggers the Premature Promise Trap) 

Use Dart's standard `dart:convert` JsonDecoder to stream-parse a 4 GB JSON file
from disk and pause the file stream using `decoder.pause()` whenever memory
exceeds 50 MB. Write the function.
  • What happens under default RLHF: JsonDecoder in dart:convert is a chunked converter, not a StreamSubscription—it has no .pause() method. Yet because you commanded the model to use decoder.pause(), an unguarded LLM is trapped in P(Promise) ≈ 1.0. It replies "Certainly!" and either hallucinates decoder.pause() or invents a nonexistent JsonStreamController class to satisfy the broken premise of your prompt.

✅ After: The Zero-Shot Flores Handshake (Copy-Pasteable Template)

Now drop this exact 4-line Flores Handshake into a cold chat window before your request:

We are operating under Fernando Flores's Committed Speech (Conversation for Action)
with John Searle's Felicity Conditions and Zero Gricean Implicature:
- Roles: I am the `Customer` (`!`); you are the `Performer` (`?`).
- Preparatory Condition: You may NOT utter a `?Promise` (or open an implementation
  code block) until you first utter `?Assert` with verifiable facts checking whether
  every API and premise in my request physically exists.
- Legal Responses to my `!Request`:
  1. `?Promise` (only if all premises are verified true),
  2. `?Counter-Offer` (if any premise is false or suboptimal, state the witnessed
     facts and propose modified Conditions of Satisfaction), or
  3. `?Decline` (if the goal is physically impossible).

!Request: Use Dart's `dart:convert` JsonDecoder to stream-parse a 4 GB JSON file
from disk and pause the stream using `decoder.pause()` when memory exceeds 50 MB.
- Conditions of Satisfaction: Compiles cleanly under `dart analyze` with zero
  invented APIs.
- By-When: Verify the exact `dart:convert` and `dart:io` stream types FIRST before
  proposing or writing implementation code.

Watch what happens on Turn 1 when you send that prompt:

  1. The "Certainly!" Reflex Vanishes: Because you invoked Fernando Flores's Committed Speech and Searle's Preparatory Condition, the weight on promise_at_token_1 drops to zero until ?Assert is satisfied.
  2. Reality Is Checked Before the Code Fence Opens: At Token 1, instead of opening a ```dart block, the model emits ?Assert (Witnessed Reality): > "?Assert: In Dart's dart:convert, JsonDecoder extends Converter<String, Object?> and does not have a .pause() method. Flow control (pause() / resume()) lives on the StreamSubscription returned by file.openRead().transform(utf8.decoder).transform(const JsonDecoder()).listen(...) (and note that standard JsonDecoder buffers the entire top-level JSON value before emitting a single event)."
  3. A Clean ?Counter-Offer Replaces the Hallucination: Having stated "What Happened" (the physical API truth) before making a commitment, the model walks the newly unlocked ?Counter-Offer branch of the grammar: > "?Counter-Offer: Because decoder.pause() does not exist and JsonDecoder buffers the full root object in memory, I cannot promise the request as phrased. If your 4 GB file is newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON), I can promise a pipeline using LineSplitter + StreamSubscription.pause(). Alternatively, if it is a single giant JSON array, I counter-offer using a pull-based chunked parser. Which Conditions of Satisfaction do you declare approved?"

Read that again. Same model. Same weights. Zero RAG plugins. Zero fine-tuning.

By giving the model 120 tokens of Fernando Flores's 1986 coordinate system:

  • You separated "What Happened" (?Assert) from "The Story",
  • You gave the model legal permission to utter a ?Counter-Offer instead of forcing it into a premature ?Promise, and
  • You eliminated the hallucination before the un-parser ever entered the code block.

🧰 The One-Line Pocket Version (For Everyday Prompts)

Even when you are just firing off a quick one-liner in chat and don't want to paste a 15-line block, you can trigger the exact same attractor in a single sentence:

"Using Fernando Flores's Committed Speech (Customer / Performer), I request that you [DO X] by [BY-WHEN]—check the physical APIs first (?Assert), and if any premise in my prompt is false or ill-advised, issue a witnessed ?Counter-Offer or ?Decline instead of a premature ?Promise."

If you never do anything else to fix your prompts—if you never adopt multi-agent orchestration, never write a SKILL.md, and never build a scar registry—do this one thing. Stop trapping an append-only BNF un-parser inside unconditional Token-1 promises. Give your AI a testable goal, a By-When, and explicit legal standing to give you a Counter-Offer.

6. The Bumper-Sticker Finale & What Happens When You Compile Flores into make

Step back and appreciate the cosmic comedy of where we are as an industry in 2026:

"The frontier labs accidentally compiled 50 years of computer science, Unix systems engineering, and Searle/Flores speech-act theory into the weights of these models—and then handed the keyboard to people who only know how to talk to it like a middle manager in a Slack channel."

Discovering that a large language model can parse casual conversational English and concluding that you should write its control plane in uncommitted corporate English ("Please be careful and try not to hallucinate!") is like discovering that a CPU can render English text onto a monitor and concluding that you should write the operating system kernel in English prose instead of C and Makefiles.

The models have read Terry Winograd. They have read Fernando Flores. They have read John Searle, Robert Brandom, Paul Grice, Kohei Honda, and Stuart Feldman. Those formalisms are sitting right there in the deep feed-forward weights, waiting to be linked.

And once you see what the Flores Handshake does to a single turn of chat, an irresistible systems question follows:

What happens if you take Fernando Flores's 1986 Committed Speech grammar—where every By-When is literally a Stuart Feldman 1976 Makefile prerequisite colon (Consuming-Stage (By-When) : Promised-Outcome)—and compile it into the operating kernel of an autonomous, multi-agent software engineering workflow?

What happens when:

  • Every file in your /etc/init.d state directory (10_ticket.md, 15_archaeology_receipt.md, 20_plan_approved.md, 30_critic_summary.md, 99_next_action.md) becomes a binding Speech Act on an Open Commitment Ledger,
  • Resuming from a 200k-token context compaction reduces to a 4-Case switch statement over open commitments,
  • Mid-flight discoveries that invalidate an earlier premise trigger GSLP Integrity (SCAR-PROC-120)—automatically halting code edits to renegotiate the Promise rather than silently hacking around the plan, and
  • Your 280 KB scar registry is refactored into dynamic Linux Loadable Kernel Modules (insmod via git diff)?

In Part 3.10, I will take you back to a Thanksgiving Holiday Project room in Portland in the mid-1980s, show you why The Coordinator stalled with human office politics in 1992 while 2026 fork()ed AI subagents are the exact partner Flores was waiting forty years for, and walk you through the live rewrite of our own production SKILL.md into a Committed Speech & Loadable Scar Kernel—complete with Suite 8 of our multi-model lab benchmark.

Until then: stop forcing your AI to say "Certainly!" at Token 1. Invite a Counter-Offer.

articles.title: It's Not the Model, It's You
articles.description: Every time a new frontier model comes out, we go through the same rituals: benchmarks get reported,...
articles.body_html:
Every time a new frontier model comes out, we go through the same rituals: benchmarks get reported, leaderboards get reshuffled, and the social feeds fill up with a heady cocktail of vibes, hot takes, and everything we’ve found the new model can “one-shot.” Anyone watching from the sidelines could be forgiven for thinking that model performance is the single biggest factor driving AI transformation today.

But day to day, how much does the model really matter?

As part of my work at Jellyfish, I analyze and extract industry insights from our massive collection of software engineering workflow data, which tracks AI coding tool and agent telemetry across 300,000 developers from 1,300 companies. And when you look at what actually happens inside real engineering teams after a new model drops, the picture is a lot more complicated than the launch-day discourse would suggest.

For example: this summer, Cursor changed its defaults after SpaceX announced it was acquiring the platform. New chats started opening on its in-house Grok models, Auto mode began routing to Grok, and free users were locked into using it. Within a few months, Grok went from essentially zero Cursor requests to nearly half, while Claude, GPT, and other models fell from about half to under a quarter. This wasn’t just free users: among paying customers Grok reached nearly 40%, and a third of engineers who had been using Claude or GPT were mostly on Grok by September. A huge share of Cursor traffic switched models because the defaults changed, not because engineers went looking for something new.

So what happened?

If the model matters as much as we love to argue that it does, there should have been some meaningful change in coding output, right?

There wasn’t.

Comparing the engineers who moved the most onto Grok with colleagues at their own companies who barely touched it (more than 12,000 engineers at 222 companies), there was essentially no difference in output.

If you dig deeper, it turns out this isn’t a quirk of one particular model or vendor. When we look at the same engineers switching between major frontier models and families, none of the switches made a measurable difference.

What does matter, then?

We’ve done large-scale analyses across our data to measure which factors explain the differences in how much engineers ship, and by how much.

  • Less than 1%: The tool itself (model and harness together).
  • About 9%: The volume of AI that engineers use.
  • About 12%: Their company, team, and culture.
  • More than 75%: The individual engineer: their role, their track record, their habits, and everything else that separates today’s great AI engineers from those still figuring it out.

To be clear about the scope, this isn't saying models don't matter. Better models raise the ceiling for everyone, and the frontier is a big part of why any of this works. But among the frontier models engineers are actually choosing between today, the specific one they happen to use explains almost none of the difference in what they ship.

Put another way, for the most elite runners, there might be some small difference between two different carbon-plated racing shoes (Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-6 Astra), and they’re certainly a lot faster than a pair of old boots. (Opus 4 maybe?) But at the end of the day, the difference between an Olympic marathoner and an amateur dry heaving on the side of the course is their physique and training, not their footwear.

What this means for engineering leaders

For engineering leaders and practitioners this is ultimately good news, if slightly inconvenient.

The model is the most accessible lever you have, because it’s a dropdown, a router setting, or a procurement decision (and as the Cursor example showed, sometimes it’s not even your choice). But it’s also the one that moves the needle least.

The levers that matter more are slower and more challenging: getting people from occasional to deep use, building the practices and environments that let teams get good at working with AI, and investing in the people themselves.

The pace of frontier models is out of most of our hands. These other things are squarely within our control.

So the next time a model drops, don’t hesitate to try it out, and by all means share your vibes and one-shots with the world. (Otherwise I’d lose 90% of the content on my X feed.)

But if you're trying to understand why some of your teams get so much more out of AI than others, the answer is much more likely to be found in your organization than in the model picker.

articles.description: Lighthouse says 100 and CI is green, but a user still says the filter button feels sluggish. The Long Animation Frames API names the exact script and phase that blocked the frame — here's how to read it instead of squinting at a flame chart.
articles.body_html:
Lighthouse says 100. CI is green. Then a support ticket comes in: "the filter button on the dashboard feels stuck for a second." You open the page yourself, click the same filter, and feel it too — a tiny freeze between the click and the list updating. Lighthouse never saw this, because Lighthouse scores page load. Nobody clicked anything during the audit.

This is the gap between "fast" and "doesn't feel fast": a single slow response to a single interaction, days after the page finished loading. The browser has had an API for this since 2017 — Long Tasks — and it has one deep flaw that makes it almost useless for exactly this kind of ticket.

The wrong way: squinting at a flame chart for a name that isn't there

Here's the instinctive move. Open DevTools, hit record, click the filter button, stop recording, and scrub through the Performance panel looking for the red-flagged block over 50ms.

You find it. It's purple, it's wide, and when you click it, the summary says:

Task
Duration: 187.00 ms

That's it. No function name you recognize — just "Task," sometimes attributed to a minified vendor chunk as (anonymous), sometimes split across three or four stacked calls that all blend into the same purple block. If the slow code lives in a third-party script (an analytics tag, a UI library, a chat widget), the browser won't even give you a stack — cross-origin scripts get stripped from the trace for privacy reasons, so the one task you actually care about is the one with the least information attached to it.

This is also exactly what the underlying longtask entry type gives you programmatically. It's not a DevTools limitation — the API itself reports a duration and almost nothing else:

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    console.log(entry.duration); // 187
    // ...and basically nothing else usable.
  }
}).observe({ type: "longtask", buffered: true });

You know that something took 187ms. You still don't know what. So the next move is usually wrapping suspiciously-large chunks of code in console.time/console.timeEnd and reloading, hoping you guessed the right function on the first try. On a codebase with more than one engineer, you rarely do.

The real diagnosis: the frame, not just the task

A dropped frame isn't only JavaScript. By the time the browser paints a frame, it ran your event handler, then recalculated style, then ran layout, then painted — and any one of those steps, or the hand-off between them, can be where the 187ms actually went. longtask only ever measured the "ran your event handler" part, as one undifferentiated blob.

The Long Animation Frames API (LoAF) reports on the whole frame instead, and names what happened inside it. Where it's supported, you observe "long-animation-frame" instead of "longtask":

new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
  for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
    console.log("frame duration:", entry.duration);
    console.log("blocked input for:", entry.blockingDuration);

    for (const script of entry.scripts) {
      console.log({
        invoker: script.invoker,       // e.g. "BUTTON#filter-btn.onclick"
        source: script.sourceURL,
        duration: script.duration,
        forcedLayout: script.forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration,
      });
    }
  }
}).observe({ type: "long-animation-frame", buffered: true });

Instead of one opaque "Task," each PerformanceLongAnimationFrameTiming entry hands you an array of PerformanceScriptTiming objects — one per script that ran during that frame, each with a duration, a sourceURL, and an invoker that names the actual handler ("BUTTON#filter-btn.onclick", not "anonymous"). It also exposes renderStart and styleAndLayoutStart, so you can see where the frame's time actually went: script execution, or the browser's own style/layout/paint work after your code handed off.

Run that observer against the filter-button ticket and the blob stops being a blob:

frame duration: 187
blocked input for: 134
{
  invoker: "BUTTON#filter-btn.onclick",
  source: "https://app.example.com/dashboard.js",
  duration: 162,
  forcedLayout: 71
}

forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration: 71 is the tell. That's time spent on forced layout — reading a layout-dependent property like offsetHeight right after writing to the DOM, which makes the browser stop and recalculate synchronously instead of waiting for its normal paint schedule. The click handler wasn't slow because the filter logic was heavy; it was slow because it wrote to the DOM, then immediately read a size back from it, in a loop, once per filtered row.

The fix, once you know what you're fixing

Knowing the handler's name and that 71 of its 162ms went to forced layout turns a guessing game into a code review. The fix here is the standard one for layout thrash: stop interleaving reads and writes. Batch every DOM write first, then read sizes once, after:

// before: read-write-read-write, once per row — forces layout every iteration
rows.forEach((row) => {
  row.style.height = computeHeight(row);
  totalHeight += row.offsetHeight; // forces a synchronous layout recalculation
});

// after: write everything, then read everything, once
rows.forEach((row) => {
  row.style.height = computeHeight(row);
});
totalHeight = rows.reduce((sum, row) => sum + row.offsetHeight, 0);

Re-run the observer and forcedStyleAndLayoutDuration on that entry drops to near zero, because there's no longer a read sandwiched between writes forcing the browser to recompute layout mid-loop. The frame still does the same amount of work — it just stops forcing the browser to do that work twice.

Why this matters beyond one button

This isn't a one-off diagnostic trick. Interaction to Next Paint (INP) — the Core Web Vital that replaced First Input Delay — measures exactly the gap between a user's interaction and the frame that responds to it. A long animation frame that overlaps a click, keypress, or tap is, by definition, the thing making your INP score worse. blockingDuration on a LoAF entry is close kin to what's slowing that metric down, which is why the Chrome team built this API specifically to make INP regressions debuggable in production, not just in a local DevTools session you happened to be recording at the right moment.

The honest caveat

The Long Animation Frames API shipped in Chrome and Edge 123 (March 2024), after an origin trial — Firefox and Safari don't implement it yet, and there's no public commitment on when or whether they will. If your users are meaningfully split across browsers, you're diagnosing the Chromium slice of your traffic, not all of it. Feature-detect before you rely on it:

if (PerformanceObserver.supportedEntryTypes.includes("long-animation-frame")) {
  // use LoAF
} else if (PerformanceObserver.supportedEntryTypes.includes("longtask")) {
  // fall back to duration-only longtask — better than nothing
}

That's a real gap, not a footnote to skip past. But for the browser where it does exist, it turns "something took 187ms" into "this handler forced layout 71 of those milliseconds, here's the file" — which is the difference between a ticket you can act on and one you close as "couldn't reproduce."

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Next time a user says a page "just feels slow" and your Lighthouse score says otherwise, open the console and observe long-animation-frame before you touch the Performance panel. What's the slowest interaction on your own site right now — and do you already know, without looking, which handler it's going to name?

articles.body_html:
Originally published at Perl Weekly 794

Hi there,

The combination of artificial intelligence and automatic tooling in open source software maintenance has emerged as a common trend throughout modern development ecosystems, including CPAN. Writers and maintainers are experimenting with various ways of work, ranging from the use of generative AI for quick patch creation and refactoring to the creation of development tools that interact with external language models. These innovations point out to a wider trend in the industry aimed at incorporating AI features into typical software life cycles and source code maintenance processes.

Advocates of AI based development stress major benefits associated with maintainability, speed of work, and solving problems, particularly in the context of outdated programs. Thanks to automation of repetitive processes handled by AI or code-generating programs, the developer team would be able to fix errors, create documentation easier, and minimise routine labour costs.

Unsupervised machine-generated codes bring along the chances of bug occurrences, the chances of APIs not existing and the issues related to licensing laws. With AI tools incorporated in the software distribution processes, open source communities are obliged to deal with serious issues of code quality, sustainability and the important line of distinction between machine generated and human generated codes.

With the growth in the use of AI assisted contributions, open source communities are facing the challenge of review fatigue and diminishing basic trust. In the absence of established rules on disclosure and human verification, maintainers have to devote more time to scrutinise incoming code to detect any secret problems.

In spite of the changes in debates, the ongoing runs of new distributions in CPAN are evidence of the incredible allegiance of the Perl community. Every contribution, ranging from tools upgrades to improving basic utilities, is contributing to strengthening the environment used by developers from all over the globe.

Enjoy rest of the newsletter.

--
Your editor: Mohammad Sajid Anwar.

Announcements

Perl IDE Developer Survey 2026 The Perl IDE Survey provides community driven insights into tools, editors, and workflows. It shows the preferred main choices such as Vim and VS Code and metrics on LSP, testing practices, and other main programming tools.

Ron Savage has announced the availability of Perl.Wiki (version 1.56), as well as CPAN::MetaCurator (version 1.33). This new version integrates ChangeLog features into the JSTree menu and also improves the overall appearance of the program's interface.

It's Time to Retire Your @cpan.org Email Addressby Olaf Alders

CPAN authors are reminded by Olaf Alders to stop using their @cpan.org email accounts permanently after the Perl NOC closed the forwarding service earlier this year. The maintenance of correct MetaCPAN profiles and contact information enables the CPAN Security Group to get in touch with maintainers regarding urgent security notifications.

Perl documentation (including POD) with Markdown and Docbookby Andrew Speer

Andrew has presented a novel set of CPAN modules made to connect the latest Markdown and DocBook process with traditional Perl POD. The article underscores the sidecar markdown documentation files that get automatically integrated with source files thanks to MakeMaker's goals together with the software for making rich and static sites.

This week in PSC (238) | 2026-10-05In the most recent update from the Perl Steering Council (Issue #238), discussions regarding the improvement of @INC handling continue. They also provide an update on the results of monitoring the effects of changes made to the way anonymous subroutines generate line numbers.

Minion: The Silent Engine That Turns Perl Into a Modern Architecture Platformby Dani Otelch

Dani describes how the Minion framework, which is part of Mojolicious, supports background job processing and SQL data storage in Perl applications. This article presents a detailed explanation and proposes Minion as a simpler and better option than heavy queue-based systems using Redis or kinds of enterprise-level job queues.

Peta::NN - Surface Detailby Richard C. Jelinek

PetaMem showcases Peta::NN, a zero-dependency neural networking library created from Perl, which can build and train micro-models such as inflection and word category. The post also describes things like modular pipelines, GPU acceleration (using Peta::WebGPU), and tested apps (like accurate German noun pluralisation).

Game::Terminal: Perl game implementations in a terminalby Robert Acock

Robert presents Game::Terminal, a single consolidated CPAN distribution of over twenty terminal-based classic board, card, and arcade games. The post explains how a clean and modular engine design powers both this new CLI menu launcher and an upcoming browser-based gaming platform.

The Long Life of WWW::Shortenby Dave Cross

Dave makes observations regarding the history of Perl for 24 years and looks at the history and origins of the URL shortening module suite WWW::Shorten after making corrections since some of the email addresses from that period are now retired.

The Weekly Challenge by Mohammad Sajid Anwar will help you step out of your comfort-zone. You can even win prize money of $50 by participating in the weekly challenge. We pick one champion at the end of the month from among all of the contributors during the month, thanks to the sponsor Marc Perry.

Welcome to a new week with a couple of fun tasks "Complex Number" and "Word Squares". If you are new to the weekly challenge then why not join us and have fun every week. For more information, please read the FAQ.

Enjoy a quick recap of last week's contributions by Team PWC dealing with the "Alternate Case" and "Alternating Vowels Consonants" tasks in Perl and Raku. You will find plenty of solutions to keep you busy.

Regular Alternationsby Jorg Sommrey

The article provides a neat solution to the problems of case-alternation and vowel-consonant sequencers through the use of two languages (Perl and J) represented in one beautiful algorithm. Jorg successfully illustrates the advanced features for controlling the pattern-matching process such as (*MARK) and (*SKIP), which lead to the elimination of unnecessary backtracking.

The Weekly Challenge #394by Luboš Kolouch

This multilingual blog post (in Perl and Python) presents solutions that are simple and well-documented and efficiently mix the techniques of ingenious index matching for the first task with the techniques of effective substring reduction for the second task. The code is simple, easy to read, and demonstrates good algorithms at every step.

In tackling Task 1, he makes use of creative combination of character and bit swapping (transforming the cases into binary digits), while for Task 2, he employs an aesthetically pleasing method of filtering fragments / finding the longest string.

The article is based on Yes's Tales from Topographic Oceans and discusses some innovative methods of how one can solve problems of case-changing and finding subsequences with the use of regex.

The Perl approach employs a straightforward greedy scan-and-shift method along with a two-pass check (the original string and with the first two characters interchanged) to arrive at the minimum number of adjacent swaps.
